## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/process
How an Epoxy Floor Gets Built | Final Finish Edmonton

The sequence How a floor actually goes. Six steps, in this order. Installation usually runs two days, and it varies with the concrete underneath. Final Finish · Edmonton 01 A free estimate Send photos of the floor, or book a visit. Either works, and both are free. Denis wants to see the concrete, what is on it now, and any cracks you already know about. 02 Grinding The slab is ground to open the surface so the coating can bond. It is loud, dusty work, and the room has to be empty before it starts. 03 Cosmetic crack filling Visible cracks are filled so they do not read through the finish. If something turns up that is structural rather than cosmetic, you hear about it then, not later. 04 The flake broadcast Flake is broadcast into the coat while it is still open. This is where the colour and the pattern of the floor are set. 05 The scrape Once it has set, the surface is scraped back. That is what turns a loose broadcast into a flat floor you can walk on and clean. 06 The top coat The last coat goes over everything. Where a room needs more grip, an anti-slip top coat goes on instead, and that is a decision we make with you. Two things this page will not tell you: when you can park on it, and what it costs. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/auto-shop-floor-coating/
Auto Shop Floor Coating Planning | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor What an auto shop floor has to survive A service bay floor takes more than almost any other: motor oil, brake fluid, coolant, battery acid, solvents, degreasers, hot tires, jack stands, lift posts, creepers, and dropped tools, every day. A coating turns bare, stained concrete into a surface that sheds fluids, cleans quickly, and reflects light. Getting there means choosing the system for those exposures and planning the work around the bays. Final Finish’s commercial work covers surface preparation, crack filling, and anti-slip finishes. Fluids and chemical resistance Every coating resists some chemicals better than others. Brake fluid and some solvents are harder on coatings than water-based fluids. The product documents include chemical resistance information, often as a table of substances and exposure times. Ask for it, check it against what your shop actually uses, and plan for prompt cleanup. A spill wiped up in minutes is a different exposure from a puddle left over a weekend. Keep safety data sheets for the coating products as well as the shop’s own chemicals. The CCOHS guide to safety data sheets explains what they contain, and Alberta’s OHS Code on chemical hazards sets the workplace rules. Hot tires, lifts, and point loads Hot tires. Vehicles coming in off hot pavement can soften some top coats and leave marks. The top coat choice matters most here. The hot-tire pickup guide explains why. Lifts. Two-post and four-post lift bases concentrate load and are anchored to the slab. Coating around anchored equipment needs a plan: coat before the lift goes in, or cut in neatly around the base. Jack stands and creepers. Point loads and hard casters wear top coats. Plates under stands help. Dropped tools. Chips happen. A flake floor hides them better than a light solid colour, and small chips can be repaired. Washdown, detailing, and grip Detailing bays and wash areas are wet most of the day, and wet, glossy coatings can be slippery. The CCOHS guidance on preventing slips, trips, and falls notes that most workplace falls happen on level floors, from slips and trips. An anti-slip top coat in wet zones and walkways adds grip. Drains and trench drains need clean terminations, and water should run toward them, not away. The slip resistance guide covers texture options for wet floors. Light floors for bright bays A light solid colour bounces light back up under vehicles and into the bay, which helps technicians see. The trade-off is that light floors show tire marks and fluid stains sooner. Many shops pair a light colour in the work zones with a darker colour or flake in the traffic lanes. Bay lines and safety markings can be part of the system. The solid-colour commercial guide has more on colour choices. Oil already in the concrete An older shop floor has years of drips soaked into it. Coating over oil-soaked concrete is where many shop floors fail, because the coating cannot bond to a surface that keeps bleeding oil back up. The preparation has to deal with it: degreasing, grinding, and in heavily soaked spots, further treatment or repair until the concrete is sound and clean. Ask how contaminated areas will be handled and how the crew will judge them ready. The oil stain guide goes into the options. The customer side of the counter A shop floor is also part of what customers see. A clean, bright floor in the bays and the waiting area tells people the work is done with care. If the shop has a showroom or reception, it can carry a more decorative finish than the service bays, while the bays get the grip and top coat they need. Keeping it looking new Grit is what dulls a coated floor, so sweeping or scrubbing it out daily does more than anything else. Clean fluids up as they happen, use a neutral cleaner rather than harsh solvents for routine mopping, and keep an eye on the busiest bays. A worn top coat can usually be renewed before the wear reaches the layers below. The scratch care guide covers routine upkeep. Downtime is a plan, not a hope A closed bay is not billing. Coating work needs empty bays, time for preparation, and time to cure before vehicles return. Plan it around your quietest days, and phase it if bays can be taken out of service a few at a time. Ask for the schedule in writing: when each bay goes down, when it can be walked on, and when it takes vehicles. Our commercial downtime guide walks through it. Getting a quote Send photos of each bay, the lifts, the drains, and the worst stains through the quote form , with a note on the fluids you handle and when the shop can close. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit. More on commercial epoxy flooring in Edmonton . Questions people ask Will brake fluid damage an epoxy floor? Brake fluid is harder on many coatings than water-based fluids, especially if it is left to sit. Check the product's chemical resistance information against the fluids your shop uses, and clean spills promptly. Can a shop floor be coated around a car lift? Yes. Either the floor is coated before the lift goes in, or the coating is cut in neatly around the base and anchors. Tell your contractor about every lift and anchor, and any plans to move them. Is an epoxy floor slippery in a detailing bay? A smooth, glossy coating can be slippery when wet. An anti-slip top coat in wet zones and walkways adds grip, and the floor should drain water away quickly. How long will my bays be out of service? It depends on the size of the shop, the condition of the concrete, and whether the work is phased. Plan it as a written schedule that shows when each bay closes, when it can be walked on, and when it takes vehicles again. Commercial epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · What a safety data sheet contains and how to use it. Alberta OHS Code: Chemical hazards and harmful substances Government of Alberta · Workplace rules for chemical hazards. CCOHS: Prevention of slips, trips and falls Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Walking surfaces, housekeeping, and footwear in slip and fall prevention. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/barn-farm-shop-floor-coating/
Barn and Farm Shop Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor What makes a farm shop floor different A farm shop is a garage, a workshop, and sometimes a wash bay in one building, at a bigger scale. The floor takes tractor tires, dropped parts, fuel, hydraulic oil, and washdown water, often in a building that is heated only some of the time. A coating can handle that, but the system and the preparation have to be chosen for it. Barns, workshops, and shops are among the spaces Final Finish coats. Heavy equipment and point loads Tractors, loaders, and trailers bring weight and grit. Plan for: Hot tires. Tires coming in off hot pavement can soften some top coats and lift marks. The hot-tire pickup guide explains why the top coat choice matters. Point loads. Jack stands, lift pads, and implement stands concentrate weight. Ask how the system handles them, and put plates under stands. Dropped steel. Chips happen where heavy parts fall. A textured flake floor hides small impacts better than a thin, glossy solid colour, and small chips can be repaired. Tracks and chains. Anything steel-tracked, chained, or dragged will damage a coating. Keep it off the coated area or plan a separate zone. Fuel, oil, fertilizer, and other chemicals Spills are part of farm work. A coated floor keeps them on the surface so they can be cleaned, a big step up from bare concrete that soaks up everything. Coatings still have limits: some chemicals will soften or stain a given product if they sit. Ask for the chemical resistance information in the product documents, and plan to clean spills promptly. Keep the safety data sheets for what is stored on the floor, and for the coating products used. The CCOHS guide to safety data sheets explains what they contain and how to use them. Water, washdown, and grip A shop floor that gets hosed down or tracks in snow needs grip. Smooth, wet epoxy can be slippery. An anti-slip top coat adds texture where people walk, and flake adds some texture on its own. The CCOHS guidance on preventing slips, trips, and falls is written for workplaces, and a working shop is one. It names the walking surface, housekeeping, and footwear as the factors that matter. Our slip resistance guide covers the options. Plan a wash bay as its own zone: more grip, a drain, and a coating that ends cleanly at the drain so water never gets under an edge. Zones in a working shop A big shop rarely uses its whole floor the same way. Thinking in zones makes the system choices clearer: The service area. Heavy equipment, jack stands, and dropped parts. A tough top coat and a finish that hides chips. The wash bay. Water all day. More grip, a drain, and clean edges. Storage and parts. Lighter traffic, and a bright floor makes small parts easier to find. The entry, office, or lunch corner. People in boots coming in from outside. Grip at the door and a floor that cleans up quickly. The zones can share one system with different top coats or textures, or be separated with a line or a colour change. Doors, aprons, and the edge of the outdoors The big overhead door is where snow, mud, and gravel come in. The concrete apron outside is exterior concrete and is usually left uncoated, while the coating inside should stop at a clean, sealed edge at the door. Expect the first few metres inside the door to take the most wear. Plan grip there, and a mat or grate if the door stays open in wet weather. Cold shops and seasonal heat Coatings need warmth to cure. An unheated shop in winter is too cold for most products, and a shop heated only when someone is working swings between temperatures. Plan the install for when the building can be held inside the product’s range, or for the warmer months. The cold-weather guide explains the limits. If the shop has in-floor heat, see coating a heated garage floor . Big floors, real logistics Large shops raise practical questions early: Clearing. Equipment, parts, and storage all need somewhere to go during the install. Power. Grinders and dust collection need electrical service. Ask what the crew needs and where it will plug in. Access. The route in, where the crew parks, and where materials are mixed. Phasing. A floor too big to empty at once can sometimes be done in sections. Ask how the joins between sections are finished. Workers and safety If the operation employs waged, non-family workers, Alberta’s occupational health and safety rules apply to that workplace. The Government of Alberta’s farm and ranch OHS page explains who is covered. A coated floor with the right grip, kept clean, is part of a safer shop. Getting started Send photos of the shop floor, the doors, the drains, and any damage through the quote form , with the size of the building and how it is heated. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit. Edmonton is home base, so ask whether your location is in range . See also workshop floor coating and residential epoxy flooring , which covers barns and workshops. Questions people ask Can a tractor drive on an epoxy floor? Rubber-tired equipment can drive on a coated floor chosen for it, with a top coat suited to hot tires and plates under stands. Steel tracks, chains, and dragged implements will damage any coating. Does a shop floor need an anti-slip top coat? Where the floor gets wet, oily, or snowy, yes, at least in walkways and wash areas. A smooth, wet coating can be slippery, and an anti-slip top coat adds grip. Flake adds some texture on its own. Can an unheated shop be coated in winter? Usually not until the building can be held inside the coating's temperature range for the install and the cure. Many owners plan an unheated shop for the warmer months. Will fuel and hydraulic oil damage a coated floor? A coating keeps spills on the surface where they can be cleaned, unlike bare concrete. Some chemicals can still soften or stain a coating if they sit, so check the product's chemical resistance information and clean spills promptly. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading CCOHS: Prevention of slips, trips and falls Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Walking surfaces, housekeeping, and footwear in slip and fall prevention. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · What a safety data sheet contains and how to use it. Occupational health and safety: Farm and ranch Government of Alberta · Who Alberta's OHS rules cover on farms and ranches. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/basement-concrete-floor-coating/
Basement Floor Coating Basics | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A basement coating should be the last decision in a short chain, not the first. Begin by deciding whether the room has a water problem, a concrete problem, or simply an unfinished surface. A coating can change colour, cleanability, texture, and light reflection. It cannot redirect groundwater, repair a failed drain, or make an unsound slab sound. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . 1. Rule out active water entry Inspect after snowmelt or heavy rain if possible. Record where dampness appears: at a wall-floor joint, around a penetration, beneath stored objects, or across the open slab. Photograph mineral deposits, dark areas, peeling paint, and previous patches. Note sump operation, plumbing leaks, downspout issues, and whether exterior drainage work is underway. This distinction matters because a moisture reading does not identify the source of liquid water. ASTM F2170 measures relative humidity inside a concrete slab at the time of testing; ASTM explicitly notes that results describe the slab’s moisture condition only when the test is performed ( ASTM F2170-19a ). Active leakage therefore calls for building or drainage diagnosis before a flooring specification. Stop the coating conversation temporarily if water is visibly entering, puddles recur without an indoor spill, or the proposed fix is described only as “sealing it in.” Resolve the source, allow the assembly to stabilize, and then reassess. 2. Map the slab rather than judging one clean patch Empty enough of the room to see the perimeter and the areas beneath rugs, cabinets, or old flooring. Mark the following on a simple sketch: cracks, including whether their edges are level or offset; hollow, weak, flaking, or spalled concrete; old adhesive, paint, curing compound, or unknown sealer; floor drains, control joints, columns, and penetrations; low areas that hold wash water; repairs that differ in colour or texture from the original slab. ACI’s current concrete-repair guide treats condition evaluation, removal of unsound concrete, material selection, surface preparation, and quality control as connected parts of a repair project ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). That is a useful mindset for a basement: do not select a finish until the repair scope is visible. A crack is not automatically a coating disqualifier. What matters is why it exists, whether it moves, whether water passes through it, and how the proposed repair will interact with the finished surface. An offset crack, recurring wet crack, or widespread deterioration deserves evaluation beyond a cosmetic fill. 3. Ask for a defined moisture test and an acceptance rule “We checked for moisture” is incomplete. A useful proposal states: the test method and edition; the number and placement of test locations; when the readings will be taken; the product manufacturer’s acceptable limits; what changes if a result exceeds those limits. In-situ relative-humidity testing under ASTM F2170 is quantitative and uses probes placed in the slab. It is different from a handheld surface reading or an informal plastic-sheet observation ( ASTM F2170-19a ). The number alone is not a universal pass/fail score: compare the documented result with the written requirements for the complete proposed system. For an older slab, ask whether a vapour retarder is known to exist beneath it. “Unknown” is a legitimate answer and should remain a documented uncertainty, not be converted into a guess. 4. Define what the room must tolerate The right finish for a mechanical room may be wrong for a bedroom or workshop. Write down actual use before discussing chemistry. Basement use Conditions to disclose Decisions to settle Laundry or utility Drips, drain access, appliance movement Edge details, repairs, cleaning method Home gym Rubber equipment, point loads, sweat, mats Texture, mat compatibility, maintenance Workshop Oils, rolling tools, dropped objects Chemical exposure, impact expectations, repairability Family or finished room Occupancy, furniture, adjacent HVAC returns Odour plan, appearance sample, return-to-use criteria Storage Shelving anchors, cardboard, limited airflow Moisture history, access, practical cleanability Avoid promises such as “waterproof,” “maintenance-free,” or “permanent” unless the proposal defines exactly what is warranted, on which substrate, and under which exclusions. 5. Plan ventilation as part of the scope Product selection, isolation, and ventilation belong in the work plan when the basement connects to occupied rooms. Health Canada recommends reducing pollutant sources and increasing ventilation during renovation activities, while following product labels and safety information ( Health Canada indoor-air guidance ). Ask where air will enter, where it will exhaust, and whether the route could send vapour or dust into another window, doorway, or air intake. Also identify occupants who may require a more conservative plan. Odour is not a reliable exposure meter; the current safety data sheet and the site-specific controls are the proper starting points. 6. Make the quote auditable Before approving work, look for a written sequence rather than a coating name alone: protect adjacent rooms and control preparation dust; identify the mechanical preparation method and target surface condition; remove or repair unsound concrete; record moisture-test results and the manufacturer’s acceptance threshold; name every primer, repair material, body coat, broadcast material, and topcoat; state how joints, edges, drains, steps, and penetrations will be treated; define inspection points before layers conceal the substrate; provide product data and safety data sheets; state conditions for foot traffic, furniture, and normal use. The best next step is a site assessment with the room exposed and its moisture history written down. Request options if the findings are uncertain: repair and proceed, test again after corrective work, select a compatible system, or postpone coating. That makes “not ready yet” an acceptable project outcome rather than a surprise found during installation. This guide is general planning information. Water entry, structural movement, hazardous materials, and product-specific safety or compatibility questions require qualified assessment and the current manufacturer instructions. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Guide to concrete condition evaluation, repair materials, surface preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170-19a: Relative Humidity in Concrete Floor Slabs ASTM International · Official page for the in-situ relative-humidity test method. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Guidance on source control and ventilation during renovations. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/cold-weather-floor-coating-edmonton/
Cold-Weather Floor Coating Tips | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor An Edmonton winter does not automatically rule out a floor-coating project. It changes what must be controlled and recorded. The important conditions are not the temperature in a weather app alone; they are the temperature and moisture conditions at the slab, in the work zone, and in the stored materials throughout preparation, application, and cure. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Environment and Climate Change Canada’s Edmonton city dataset includes daily temperature normals, extremes, and counts of cold days for the 1991–2020 normal period ( Edmonton climate normals ). That official record supports a practical conclusion: a winter quote needs a cold-weather control plan, not an assumption that an attached garage or loading area will remain suitable. Think in zones, not one thermostat reading Divide the project into four temperature zones: Outside: affects open-door events, deliveries, exhaust placement, and replacement air. Material storage: affects the temperature of resin, hardener, repair products, and aggregates before mixing. Room air: affects worker comfort, ventilation, and product cure. Concrete slab: may lag far behind a short burst of warm air and can vary near doors, walls, drains, or unheated edges. Ask the contractor which temperatures the product data sheet requires, where measurements will be taken, and how frequently they will be logged. “The garage will be heated” does not answer those questions. The winter go/no-go sheet Use a small table at the pre-start meeting and again before each coat. Check Evidence to record If it is outside the product limit Ambient air Time, location, calibrated reading Pause or correct enclosure/heating Slab surface Several readings, especially at edges and door Continue conditioning; do not average away a cold spot Relative humidity Reading in the work zone Follow product limit and condensation controls Dew-point margin Air temperature, humidity, surface temperature Do not coat where condensation risk violates instructions Material temperature Storage location and reading if required Condition materials within permitted range Forecast and door schedule Expected lows and planned openings Protect the cure period or reschedule The numbers must come from the exact products being installed. As one bounded example, the current Sikafloor-217 page shows different pot-life, foot-traffic, full-cure, and recoat times at 10°C, 20°C, and 30°C ( Sika product data ). Those values are not interchangeable with another epoxy, a polyaspartic, a repair mortar, or a primer. The example demonstrates why a generic “epoxy cures overnight” schedule is not a specification. Heating can create new variables Temporary heat should be treated as project equipment with a placement and monitoring plan. Settle these details before work: how long the space will be conditioned before preparation and application; whether equipment introduces combustion products or moisture; how fresh air will replace exhausted air without chilling the slab; who monitors conditions overnight; what happens during a power or heater failure; whether doors must open for vehicles, waste removal, or deliveries; how heaters and cords will be kept outside restricted or wet work areas. The goal is stable conditions, not the highest possible air temperature. Rapidly warming cold air can leave the concrete colder than the room. The crew should calculate and document the condensation margin required by the product data rather than relying on touch. Sequence winter logistics before mixing begins A workable Edmonton cold-weather sequence looks like this: Several days before: confirm the product-specific temperature range, arrange a safe enclosure, choose material storage, and review the forecast. Move vehicles, salt, snow, and wet mats away from the area. Before preparation: stabilize the room, inspect for water carried in by vehicles or melting snow, and measure the slab in a grid. Confirm dust-control equipment and safe exhaust routing. After preparation: prevent new condensation, tracked-in salt, or exhaust deposits from contaminating the open concrete. Recheck the substrate because preparation can reveal cracks, weak concrete, and damp areas. Before every layer: verify air, slab, humidity, and material conditions against that layer’s current product data sheet. Record batch numbers and application time so recoat decisions remain traceable. During cure: restrict doors, vehicles, washing, and foot traffic according to written criteria. Maintain the required conditions for the full period, not only until the crew leaves. Ventilation must still work in cold weather Closing every opening may conserve heat but does not substitute for an exposure-control plan. Health Canada recommends controlling pollutant sources, following label directions, and increasing ventilation during renovations ( Health Canada indoor-air guidance ). For an attached garage or occupied commercial space, ask where replacement air enters and where exhaust leaves. Check its relationship to doors, windows, soffits, and mechanical-air intakes. Identify who can enter the zone and what signs or barriers will be used. The product safety data sheets—not odour strength—should inform protective measures and occupancy decisions. Compare winter proposals on controls A credible cold-weather scope answers six questions in writing: Which exact products and product-data-sheet editions govern the work? What are the permitted air, slab, humidity, and condensation conditions for each layer? Who records those conditions, and can the owner see the log? How are materials stored and conditioned? How are heat and ventilation balanced safely? What is the contingency if conditions leave the permitted range? Do not accept a warmer-season timeline copied into a winter quote without these dependencies. The project may proceed, change products, need longer conditioning, or be postponed. A planned no-go decision is better than forcing a layer onto a slab that does not meet its written requirements. This guide does not set application temperatures or safe ventilation rates. Use the current product data and safety data sheets, applicable Alberta safety requirements, and qualified site-specific advice. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Canadian Climate Normals 1991–2020: Edmonton City Environment and Climate Change Canada · Official Edmonton composite-station normals and extremes. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Guidance for source control and ventilation during renovation work. Sikafloor-217 product data Sika Corporation · Bounded manufacturer example showing temperature-dependent pot life, cure, and recoat values; not a project recommendation. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/commercial-flooring-downtime-planning/
Commercial Floor Downtime Plan | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor “How many days will we be closed?” is the wrong first scheduling question. Start with the business events that cannot overlap the work: customers crossing the area, forklifts serving a dock, sanitation cycles, emergency egress, deliveries, food preparation, patient movement, or access to electrical and mechanical rooms. Then build the coating sequence between those constraints. For local scope options, see our commercial epoxy flooring . The result is a shutdown plan with decision gates, not a promise based on a calendar alone. Create an operations map before requesting dates Walk the area with the facility lead, installer, health-and-safety contact, and the person who can authorize reopening. Mark: pedestrian, cart, pallet-jack, and vehicle routes; exits, fire equipment, panels, drains, coolers, and shutoffs; production equipment that stays, moves, or needs disconnection; adjacent occupants and shared ventilation; receiving hours, cleaning shifts, and contractor access; temperature-sensitive inventory; noise-, dust-, or odour-sensitive operations; the smallest zones that can function independently. Alberta’s official OHS page links the current Act, Regulation, and Code that govern Alberta workplaces ( Alberta OHS legislation ). The owner and contractors should decide who controls the work area, communicates hazards, manages simultaneous work, and verifies that required routes remain available. Break “downtime” into five clocks A proposal that lists only application time hides most schedule risk. Clock Starts when Ends when Common dependency Operational clear-out Inventory or equipment begins moving Area is released to contractor Labour, lockout, disconnection Preparation Protection and surface work begin Substrate passes inspection Removal difficulty, repairs, dust control Layer sequence First material is mixed Last specified layer is complete Recoat windows, temperature, humidity Restricted cure Last layer is placed Defined traffic is permitted Product data and actual site conditions Recommissioning Protection is removed Normal operations resume Cleaning, equipment setup, owner acceptance These clocks can overlap only when the site plan says they can. For example, moving equipment in Zone B while grinding Zone A may be possible, but only if traffic, dust, noise, and emergency access remain controlled. Product timelines are condition-dependent. As a bounded example, Sikafloor-217 lists different recoat, foot-traffic, light-traffic, and full-cure times at 10°C, 20°C, and 30°C ( Sika product data ). Those figures are not a schedule for another system; they show why the project plan must reference the exact product sheets and recorded conditions. Use gates instead of optimistic hand-offs Put an owner and required evidence beside every gate. Gate 1 — area released: equipment disposition is complete; services are isolated where required; access and emergency arrangements are active. Gate 2 — substrate accepted: preparation is complete; hidden contamination and damage have been assessed; repairs, moisture results, and surface condition are documented. Gate 3 — ready for next layer: elapsed time and ambient/substrate conditions meet the current product instructions; contamination has not occurred; any maximum recoat requirement is still satisfied. Gate 4 — restricted traffic: the named product criteria for that traffic class are met. “Dry to touch” is not automatically permission for carts, shelving, washing, or vehicle loads. Gate 5 — operational reopening: barriers can be removed; required cleaning and inspection are complete; equipment and routes are safely restored; the owner accepts outstanding items. If a gate fails, the plan needs a branch: repair and re-inspect, mechanically prepare an overdue layer as instructed, extend environmental control, reopen another zone, or move the launch date. Design zones around complete work packages Phasing reduces the area unavailable at one time but adds edges, transitions, mobilizations, and coordination. Do not divide the floor into arbitrary rectangles. Each zone should have: a safe independent entry and exit; enough room for preparation and dust collection; a deliberate termination detail between phases; a route for waste out and materials in; protection from traffic in adjacent live zones; a defined cleaning and acceptance point. A checkerboard plan usually creates more boundary and traffic problems than it solves. Long strips, complete rooms, or operational cells are often easier to isolate, but the actual choice depends on equipment, joints, drainage, and workflow. Account for the work around the coating Commercial downtime is frequently consumed by tasks omitted from the coating quote: disconnecting racks, removing old flooring, testing unknown residues, curing repair materials, relocating inventory, resetting equipment, and cleaning construction dust. CCOHS recommends keeping aisles and exits clear, providing orderly storage, and cleaning spills promptly as part of workplace housekeeping ( CCOHS housekeeping guide ). Translate that into the shutdown plan: designate material staging, waste routes, cord and hose management, spill response, and who maintains adjacent live areas. Also list the facilities that cannot be isolated—washrooms, coolers, server rooms, loading docks—and determine whether coating work can proceed safely around them. Build the run sheet backwards Begin with the required reopening event and work backwards: normal operations restored; equipment and inventory returned; owner closeout and cleaning complete; permitted traffic threshold reached; final coat placed under acceptable conditions; preceding recoat gates met; repairs and prepared substrate accepted; area cleared and controlled. Add contingency at the steps with real uncertainty, especially removal, repairs, moisture findings, temperatures, and maximum recoat windows. Name one decision-maker who can trade scope, phase, or reopening date if an assumption fails. The final schedule should include product-sheet references, shift times, condition logs, inspection gates, communication contacts, and alternative routes. That document is more useful than a single “three-day system” label because it connects the material sequence to the way the facility actually operates. This is planning guidance, not a safe-work procedure. The employer, prime contractor, and qualified project team must apply current Alberta requirements, product safety data, and site-specific controls. Commercial epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta OHS Act, Regulation and Code Government of Alberta · Official access point for Alberta workplace health and safety legislation. CCOHS: Workplace Housekeeping—Basic Guide Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Guidance on access, storage, spill control, and housekeeping. Sikafloor-217 product data Sika Corporation · Bounded product example showing that recoat and traffic times depend on temperature. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-cracks-spalling-floor-coating/
Cracks and Spalling Before Coat | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Cracks and spalls are not one defect. A narrow dormant crack, a moving joint, a thin scaled surface, and a deep patch around corroding reinforcement need different responses. Covering every line with the same filler may improve a photograph while leaving the cause and movement unchanged. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . ACI’s concrete-repair guide organizes repair work around evaluation, selection of repair strategy and materials, preparation, application, and quality control ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). Use that sequence before deciding what the finished floor should look like. Name the condition accurately Crack: a separation in the concrete. Record width, length, location, moisture, edge level, and whether it changes. Control or contraction joint: an intentional plane intended to manage where shrinkage cracking occurs. It is a floor detail, not automatically a defect. Construction joint: where separate concrete placements meet. Its movement and loading conditions may differ from a random crack. Scaling: loss of a thin surface layer, often seen as flaking or a rough shallow area. Spall: a localized loss of concrete with measurable depth. Its edges may be weak or undercut, and the damaged area may extend beyond what is visually missing. Delamination: a separation below the visible surface. The top may remain in place but sound hollow or break during preparation. Pop-out: a small conical fragment that separates, often around a particle. Multiple pop-outs should be mapped rather than treated as isolated pinholes. These labels do not establish a cause. They simply prevent unlike conditions from being priced as one bucket of “crack repair.” Use a triage path 1. Is there displacement or ongoing movement? Compare the two sides of the crack with a straightedge. Look for offset, crushed edges, repeated repairs that reopened, and a line continuing through walls or structural elements. A coating contractor should not be expected to diagnose structural movement from appearance alone. Escalate significant displacement or suspected structural behaviour to an appropriately qualified professional. 2. Is water or contamination involved? Record dampness, mineral deposits, oil, cleaning chemicals, and any history of leakage. A wet crack may be a pathway or merely a visible low point; it requires investigation before a dry repair product is selected. 3. Is the surrounding concrete sound? The repair boundary should not be drawn only around the missing piece. Preparation can reveal weak edges or hidden delamination. ACI includes evaluation and removal of unsound concrete as part of the repair process, not as optional cosmetic work ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). 4. Must the line remain a joint? Ask how intentional joints will be treated. Filling a moving joint rigidly, bridging it, or carrying it through the coating are different design decisions with different appearance and maintenance consequences. The proposal should name the chosen detail. Match the intervention to the observation Observed condition Information needed before repair Coating-plan implication Fine, level crack Movement history, moisture, contamination May remain visible or reflect; define treatment and expectation Reopened previous fill Prior material, movement, edge condition Remove failed material and reassess cause Offset or widening crack Structural context and monitoring Obtain qualified evaluation before cosmetic work Shallow scaling Depth and soundness after preparation Remove weak surface; verify remaining substrate Deep spall Extent, cause, reinforcement, repair depth Select repair method and cure/overcoat sequence Hollow area Delamination boundary Remove or evaluate unsound section before coating Wet crack Water source and moisture condition Resolve water issue and check system compatibility No table can select a repair product from a photograph. Repair materials differ in thickness range, substrate-conditioning requirements, cure, movement capacity, and compatibility with later layers. Capture those requirements from the current manufacturer documents. What good preparation looks like Preparation must create sound boundaries, remove contaminants and weak material, and leave the surface required by the repair or coating. ICRI 310.2R summarizes the capabilities, operating requirements, and limitations of concrete preparation methods and provides benchmark profiles for specification and verification ( ICRI 310.2R ). That means “grind and fill cracks” is too vague. The scope should say: which cracks, joints, spalls, and weak areas are included; how repair boundaries will be established; how dust and debris will be removed; the repair product and permitted placement range; required concrete and ambient conditions; cure or overcoat criteria before the next layer; how repaired areas will be checked; what unit rate or approval process applies to concealed damage. Set appearance expectations before coating Even a technically appropriate repair can telegraph as a colour, texture, or level variation. A thin finish shows substrate irregularity differently from a thicker broadcast system. Movement can reappear. Patching every visible mark does not make an old slab visually equivalent to new concrete. Decide which outcome matters most: preserving functional joints, reducing trip edges, producing a uniform decorative field, resisting a known exposure, or making future repairs accessible. Request a sample or mock-up when appearance at repairs is important, and document which defects are accepted rather than repaired. The responsible next step is a marked floor plan with each condition classified and a written repair allowance for what preparation may reveal. That turns hidden deterioration into a managed project risk instead of an argument after the surface is opened. This guide cannot diagnose structural movement, corrosion, or water entry. Seek qualified evaluation for displaced cracks, exposed reinforcement, widespread delamination, or recurring moisture, and follow current repair-product instructions. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Current guide covering concrete evaluation, repair selection, preparation, application, and quality control. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Official description of preparation methods, limitations, and benchmark surface profiles. Keep exploring Related floor guides Repair Mortars Before Coating ↗ Diamond Grinding for Floor Prep ↗ Repair or Replace a Coated Floor ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-moisture-testing-floor-coatings/
Concrete Moisture Testing Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A concrete moisture test is useful only when three things are named: the method, the installation conditions, and the coating system’s acceptance limit. A meter swept across the surface may help an assessor compare locations, but it does not become an ASTM test merely because it displays a number. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . Moisture testing also does not answer every water question. It does not locate a plumbing leak, prove exterior drainage is sound, or guarantee how a slab will behave forever. First decide what you are trying to learn Before testing, write the decision the result will inform: Can the specified primer or coating be installed under the manufacturer’s published moisture limit? Are readings consistent across the proposed work area? Has a recently uncovered or repaired area reached the condition required for the next step? Does an unexpected wet location require water-source investigation? Is a mitigation option needed, and what evidence supports it? ASTM F2170 states that moisture permeating from concrete can affect flooring and coatings, and that internal relative-humidity testing is one method manufacturers may require before installation ( ASTM F2170-19a ). It also states an essential limitation: results indicate the slab condition at the time of the test. Do not mix unlike methods Method What the official method addresses What to request in the report In-situ relative humidity Quantitative percent relative humidity within the slab under ASTM F2170 Probe locations, slab details, equilibration and readings required by the edition used Calcium-chloride test Moisture vapour emission from a prepared concrete surface under ASTM F1869 Test area preparation, exposure period, mass data, calculated result and locations Handheld electrical meter Instrument-specific comparative or screening reading Model, mode, calibration/check procedure, locations, and stated limitation Plastic-sheet observation Qualitative observation under a specified procedure Procedure, duration, conditions, observations; not a numeric substitute ASTM F1869 is a distinct standard for measuring moisture vapour emission rate from a concrete subfloor using anhydrous calcium chloride ( ASTM F1869-23 ). Its result and units cannot be renamed “relative humidity,” just as an in-situ RH result cannot be reported as an emission rate. The product manufacturer may require one method, several methods, or additional conditions. Use the current documents for the exact primer and complete floor system. Build a defensible test plan A test plan should exist before holes are drilled or kits are opened. Include: Drawing: outline the work area, slab boundaries if known, exterior edges, drains, previous flooring, repairs, and suspicious locations. Method and edition: cite the complete standard designation rather than “moisture test.” Tester and equipment: identify who performs the work and how equipment conformity or calibration is documented. Quantity and distribution: follow the test method and project specification; add justified locations for wet observations or separate slab areas. Building conditions: document whether the space is operating at expected service conditions and whether old flooring was recently removed. Acceptance criteria: quote the system manufacturer’s current limit and any required preparation or mitigation. Decision path: say what happens after a pass, a fail, a mixed set, or an invalid test. Without an acceptance criterion, testing produces data but no project decision. Without a location map, a low result from one corner can be incorrectly applied to the entire floor. Read the report critically Look for raw readings as well as a pass/fail label. Ask: Do probe or kit locations match the floor plan? Are the units correct for the method? Were required time and environmental conditions recorded? Is any result missing, damaged, or identified as invalid? Do results cluster near doors, exterior walls, drains, or former floor coverings? Is the quoted acceptance limit traceable to the exact proposed product and current data sheet? Does the report separate observation from interpretation? Do not average a high location out of existence. A mixed result may indicate different slab placements, exposure history, coverings, vapour-retarder conditions, or a localized water source. It may justify more testing or investigation rather than immediate coating. Connect moisture to the rest of the substrate Moisture is one input. The slab must also be sound, clean, appropriately profiled, and repaired. ACI’s concrete-repair guide connects condition evaluation, material selection, surface preparation, and quality control ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). A passing moisture result does not override oil contamination, weak laitance, moving cracks, or an incompatible repair. Likewise, a result above a standard system’s published limit does not prove the only answer is a “moisture barrier.” Ask for the named mitigation system, its own substrate requirements and limits, the test evidence supporting its use, and how joints or water entry are treated. Compare postponement, source correction, retesting, and a manufacturer-approved alternative. The minimum documentation to keep Retain the test plan, floor map, raw results, photographs, equipment identifiers, applicable product data sheets, and the final decision. Record which areas were covered by the conclusion and which remained untested. If construction conditions or the selected system change, reassess whether the old results still answer the new question. The practical standard for a proposal is simple: another informed person should be able to trace the test location, method, reading, product limit, and resulting action without relying on memory. Moisture standards contain detailed procedures and safety provisions that this overview does not reproduce. Testing, drilling, water-source diagnosis, and coating selection should be performed by competent parties using current standards and manufacturer instructions. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ASTM F2170-19a: Relative Humidity in Concrete Floor Slabs ASTM International · Official in-situ relative-humidity test method and significance statement. ASTM F1869-23: Moisture Vapor Emission Rate ASTM International · Official calcium-chloride moisture-vapour-emission test method. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete condition, repair, preparation, and quality-control context. Keep exploring Related floor guides Basement Floor Coating Basics ↗ Garage Floor Prep in Edmonton ↗ Primer in a Floor Coating System ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-polishing-vs-floor-coating/
Concrete Polish vs Floor Coat | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor The first question is not “Which lasts longer?” It is “Do you want the concrete itself to be the finished surface, or do you want a separate material system over it?” Polishing refines and exposes the slab. A resinous coating builds a film or system above the slab. That basic choice shapes appearance, repairs, moisture tolerance, maintenance, and future changes. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . The short comparison Decision factor Polished concrete Resinous floor coating Visual character Reveals aggregate, cracks, patches, and slab variation Can introduce opaque colour, flake, quartz, gloss, or texture Relationship to slab The slab becomes the finish A bonded layer is added to the slab Defect visibility Repairs and historic marks remain part of the surface Some variation can be visually reduced, but movement may still reflect Chemical exposure Depends on concrete, densifier/sealer, and maintenance System can be selected for named exposures using product data Texture Developed through the grinding/polishing sequence and any treatment Adjusted through aggregate, broadcast, film build, and topcoat Future work Regrinding or local repair affects appearance Local recoating or patching may differ in colour and texture Moisture Still requires slab and treatment evaluation Must meet the complete system’s moisture requirements This is not a universal winner table. It is a way to identify which questions deserve testing and samples. Choose polishing when the slab is the design Polishing is a strong candidate when natural concrete variation is welcome, the slab is reasonably consistent, and the owner accepts that cracks, aggregate exposure, patches, and edge work will remain visible. ACI’s decorative-concrete guide covers variables such as materials, construction, finishing, protection, and maintenance that affect decorative results ( ACI PRC-310-19 ). Before choosing a sheen from a photograph, investigate: aggregate exposure in representative test areas; previous floor coverings and adhesive shadows; hardness differences between placements or repairs; edge and corner access; crack and joint appearance; existing sealers, stains, and contamination; the maintenance method available to the owner. The phrase “polished concrete” is incomplete without the intended aggregate exposure, final refinement level, treatment products, edge standard, mock-up location, and acceptance criteria. Choose a coating when the added layer has a job A coating becomes more compelling when the owner needs an opaque field, deliberate texture, a system built around a named chemical exposure, easier visual zoning, or a broadcast finish. It may also provide a clearer path to visually unify dissimilar concrete—within the limitations of movement and substrate condition. The coating route requires its own detailed choices: preparation method, target profile, repairs, primer, body coat, broadcast, topcoat, thickness, joints, and cure conditions. ICRI 310.2R explains that surface-preparation methods have different capabilities, operating requirements, and limitations, and provides profiles for specifying and verifying the prepared surface ( ICRI 310.2R ). Do not select a coating solely because the existing slab looks poor. If the concrete is unsound or moisture conditions exceed the proposed system’s limits, an opaque finish does not remove those constraints. Five questions that decide more than gloss 1. What should repairs look like? Both options inherit the slab’s cracks and patches. Polishing usually celebrates or at least reveals them. A coating may disguise colour variation, yet filled cracks can remain visible and moving cracks may reappear. ACI connects repair strategy to evaluation, preparation, application, and quality control ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). Ask for a mock-up containing a real repair, not only sound new concrete. 2. What contacts the floor? List cleaners, oils, food acids, salts, solvents, hot equipment, tyres, rubber mats, and standing water. For a coating, request manufacturer test data relevant to the actual concentration, temperature, contact time, and cleaning routine. For polished concrete, request the same clarity about any densifier, guard, or sealer and its maintenance. 3. How will slip risk be managed? “Polished” and “textured coating” are not complete slip-resistance specifications. Describe footwear, contamination, slopes, drains, cleaning, and transitions. Agree on a sample texture and a documented test or acceptance method suited to the project. 4. Who maintains it? Ask the maintenance team which machines, pads, cleaners, and skills it already has. Polished concrete may rely on a defined dust-mopping, cleaning, and periodic refinement or guard routine. A coating may require non-damaging cleaners, protection from abrasive soil, and inspection for worn topcoat or local damage. The best finish is the one the facility can maintain as specified. 5. What downtime can the operation absorb? Polishing involves repeated mechanical passes, edge work, cleaning, and treatments. Coating involves mechanical preparation, repairs, sequential layers, recoat windows, and cure gates. Compare full work plans, including equipment moves and reopening—not slogans such as “one day” or “no downtime.” Use two adjacent mock-ups For a meaningful comparison, place polishing and coating mock-ups on representative concrete. Include a crack, an edge, and a repaired area where possible. Evaluate them under the actual lighting and from normal viewing distance. Record: aggregate exposure or coating colour and texture; visibility of repairs and joints; cleanability using the planned method; slip strategy when clean and under expected contamination; edge, drain, and transition details; acceptance limits for natural variation. The decision should emerge from the room’s use and the slab’s evidence. If the natural concrete is desirable and its variation acceptable, polishing keeps that material at centre stage. If the floor needs a distinct functional layer or opaque design, a properly specified coating may fit better. In either case, the quality of evaluation, repairs, execution, and maintenance matters more than the category name. This comparison is not a project specification. Have qualified parties assess the slab, safety needs, exposures, and current manufacturer requirements before selection. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-310-19: Guide to Decorative Concrete American Concrete Institute · Official ACI guide covering decorative concrete, including polished finishes and variables affecting appearance. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Preparation methods, limitations, and profile verification for coatings and overlays. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete evaluation, repair selection, preparation, and quality-control context. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-repair-mortars-floor-coatings/
Repair Mortars Before Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A repair mortar replaces missing or removed concrete so the floor again has the shape, support, and surface needed for its next use. It is not automatically a crack filler, moisture barrier, levelling compound, or structural design solution. The correct role depends on the defect and on what will be installed above it. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . ACI’s repair guide treats condition evaluation, repair strategy, material selection, surface preparation, application, and quality control as one process ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). Skipping directly to a bag or cartridge reverses that sequence. Four jobs that are often confused Product role Typical purpose Question before coating Patching or repair mortar Rebuild a spall or removed unsound area Is the placement depth, edge detail, and loading suitable? Resurfacer or overlay Renew a larger shallow area What substrate profile and minimum thickness are required? Crack repair material Treat a crack under defined movement and moisture conditions Is the crack active, structural, wet, or an intentional joint? Underlayment or leveller Correct elevation or flatness before a finish Is it approved for the traffic and bonded coating system? One material may serve more than one role, but only its current product data establishes that. The project should name the role rather than use “repair compound” as a catch-all. Selection starts with the repair geometry Measure the defect after unsound concrete is removed, not before. Record depth, area, edge shape, slope, exposure, and whether reinforcement, joints, drains, or moving cracks are involved. A thin feather edge, deep pocket, vertical face, and broad resurfacing area impose different placement demands. ICRI 320.2R provides guidance for selecting and specifying materials for repair of concrete surfaces ( ICRI 320.2R ). A useful submittal translates that general selection task into project-specific answers: permitted minimum and maximum thickness per lift; bond or substrate-conditioning method; working time at expected material and site temperatures; shrinkage and movement considerations; compressive and flexural properties where relevant to service; moisture condition permitted during placement; cure and protection requirements; time and condition for overcoating; compatibility with the named primer and coating. Do not choose by compressive-strength number alone. A repair also has to bond, fit the geometry, tolerate the placement conditions, and accept the next layer. The repair sequence 1. Confirm the cause and boundary Map the visibly damaged area, then determine whether adjacent concrete is weak or delaminated. If corrosion, structural movement, repeated water entry, or broad deterioration is suspected, obtain the appropriate professional assessment before defining a cosmetic patch. 2. Remove unsound material Establish sound concrete and a repair shape that the selected product allows. Protect reinforcement, embedded services, joints, and adjacent finishes. ICRI 310.2R explains that surface-preparation methods differ in capabilities, operating requirements, and limitations ( ICRI 310.2R ). The method should suit the defect without creating avoidable microdamage or polishing the bond surface. 3. Prepare and condition the substrate Remove dust, debris, oil, and bond-inhibiting residues. Apply water conditioning, primer, or bonding agent only as the repair manufacturer specifies. “Clean and dry” is not universal; some cementitious materials call for a particular saturated-surface-dry condition, while resinous repairs may require a dry substrate. 4. Batch, mix, place, and finish Record lot numbers and mixing quantities. Respect water or component ratios, mixing equipment, working time, lift thickness, consolidation, and finish. Adding water to extend working time or spreading beyond permitted thickness changes the installation from the documented product procedure. 5. Cure and protect The repair may require moisture retention, temperature control, protection from traffic, or a specified wait before grinding and coating. Coordinate curing compounds carefully: a surface-applied cure may conflict with the later bond unless the system documents how it is removed or approved. 6. Verify before concealing Inspect edges, soundness, level, surface texture, cracks, and cure condition. Confirm the overcoat requirements for both the repair and the coating. Keep photographs because the repair will soon be hidden. Compatibility has two directions The repair mortar must bond to the old concrete, and the coating must bond to the repair. Ask both manufacturers’ current documents to answer: Can the coating be applied directly, or is a primer required? What repair age, moisture condition, and surface profile are acceptable? Must laitance or curing residue be mechanically removed? Does the repair contain polymer or other ingredients that change preparation? Are moisture tests interpreted differently over the repair and original slab? What happens at the edge where new mortar meets old concrete? A product described as “rapid” may gain handling strength before it reaches the condition required for a specific coating. Use the written overcoat criteria, not a generic clock. Price uncertainty honestly Preparation often reveals a larger repair than the visible spall. A sound quote identifies the included repair quantity and a controlled mechanism for extras: unit rate, allowance, photographs, owner approval, and schedule effect. That protects both parties from either burying deterioration or treating every newly found condition as an undefined change. The closeout record should contain the defect map, removal limits, repair product and lot, placement conditions, mixing notes, cure period, preparation before coating, and inspection result. That record is the practical value of a repair mortar: not merely filling a hole, but creating a documented transition from damaged concrete to a substrate the finish system is designed to accept. Repair around reinforcement, structural cracks, or widespread deterioration requires qualified design. Always follow current repair and coating manufacturer instructions and applicable safety requirements. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Current concrete repair guide covering evaluation, materials, preparation, application, and quality control. ICRI Guideline 320.2R-2018 International Concrete Repair Institute · Official guide for selecting and specifying concrete surface repair materials. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Preparation methods, limitations, and benchmark profiles. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-sealer-vs-floor-coating/
Concrete Sealer vs Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor The short answer A sealer protects concrete from water and salt getting in. A coating puts a new wearing surface on top. Sealers are thin, mostly invisible, and need reapplying. A coating system, like an epoxy flake floor, is a built-up layer that changes how the floor looks, cleans, and wears. Which one makes sense depends on what the floor faces and how you want it to look. Three things people call sealer Penetrating sealers soak into the concrete and line its pores. Silanes and siloxanes are the common ones. They repel water and salt brine and leave the surface looking much the same. They are widely used on outdoor concrete such as driveways and walks. Densifiers react with the concrete to harden the surface and cut down on dusting. They are used on bare interior floors and under polished concrete. Film-forming sealers , often acrylic, sit on top as a thin clear layer with some sheen. They wear off under traffic and tires and need reapplying. The ACI guide to protective treatments for concrete covers these families, and more, and how to choose among them for a given exposure. What a coating does differently A floor coating is a system of layers bonded to ground concrete. In a flake floor, that is a base coat, a broadcast of flake, a scrape, and a clear top coat. The result is a new surface: sealed against spills, easy to clean, and in the colour and texture you choose. The difference shows up in daily use: Stains. Oil and fluids soak into bare or sealed concrete over time. On a coating, they sit on top and wipe up. Wear. Film sealers wear through in the tire paths. A coating is built to take the traffic, and its top coat is chosen for it. Dust. Bare concrete sheds fine dust. A coating stops it. Looks. A sealer keeps concrete looking like concrete. A coating changes the floor. Salt, winter, and Edmonton garages Salt brine is the winter enemy of concrete. Alberta Infrastructure’s bulletin on de-icing chemicals explains how de-icers and freeze-thaw cycles damage concrete that stays saturated. In a garage, meltwater pools under the car and salt residue collects along the parking tracks. A penetrating sealer reduces how much brine soaks in. A coating keeps the brine on the surface, where it can be mopped away. The winter salt guide covers the damage patterns on bare slabs. Coating over a sealed floor This is the part that catches people. A penetrating or film-forming sealer that is still on the floor can stop a coating from bonding. If a garage was sealed in the past, the sealer has to come off before coating. Diamond grinding does that, and the ICRI guideline on surface preparation is the reference for preparing concrete for sealers and coatings alike. Not sure whether a floor was sealed? A simple sign is water beading on the surface instead of darkening the concrete. Tell your contractor what you know, including any product names from past owners. Driveway, garage, and basement are different jobs The same word gets used for three very different floors: The driveway is outside, in freeze-thaw and direct sun, and it has to breathe. Penetrating sealers are the usual treatment for exterior concrete, and interior floor coatings are not designed for it. The garage sits between outside and in. It takes meltwater, salt, oil, and hot tires. A sealer slows the damage; a coating changes the surface into something that cleans off. The basement is dry living space. A sealer does little there beyond dust control, while a coating turns the slab into a finished floor. Upkeep over the years A sealer is maintenance you repeat. Penetrating sealers are reapplied as their water repellency fades, and film sealers are stripped or topped up as they wear through in traffic lanes. A coating is maintenance of a different kind: regular cleaning, and in time a fresh top coat where the traffic has dulled it. A top coat can often be renewed without redoing the whole system, if it is done before wear reaches the layers below. The recoat timing guide explains why the timing matters. When each one is the right call A sealer can be the right choice when you want the floor to keep looking like plain concrete, when the goal is mainly to slow water and salt, or for outdoor slabs. A coating is the right choice when you want a clean, finished floor that resists stains, dust, and wear, and looks the part. Our comparisons of epoxy and concrete paint and polishing and coating cover the other common alternatives. Choosing for your floor Final Finish installs epoxy floor coatings, including flake and metallic systems, and prepares concrete by diamond grinding. If you are weighing a coating for a garage, basement, or shop, send photos through the quote form for a free estimate, or read about residential epoxy flooring and concrete solutions . Questions people ask Can you put epoxy over a sealed concrete floor? Not directly. A sealer still on the surface can stop a coating from bonding, so it is removed first, usually by diamond grinding. If water beads on the floor instead of darkening the concrete, there may be a sealer on it. Is a sealer enough for a garage floor? It depends on what you want. A penetrating sealer slows water and salt from soaking in, but it leaves bare concrete that still stains and sheds dust. A coating adds a wearing surface that resists stains and cleans easily. How often does a concrete sealer need reapplying? It depends on the product, the traffic, and the exposure. Film-forming sealers wear through first in tire paths and walkways. The product's documents give the expected interval between applications. Does a floor coating protect concrete from road salt? A coating keeps salt brine on the surface instead of letting it soak into the concrete, so it can be cleaned away. It still needs regular cleaning through the winter so residue does not sit on the floor. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-515.2-13: Guide to Selecting Protective Treatments for Concrete American Concrete Institute · Protective treatments against water, salts, acids, and oils. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. Alberta Infrastructure: De-Icing Concrete Government of Alberta · Technical bulletin on de-icers, concrete durability, and spring washing. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/concrete-surface-profile-csp/
Concrete Surface Profile (CSP) | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Concrete surface profile, usually shortened to CSP, describes the roughness and texture left after concrete preparation. Imagine the difference between a smooth countertop, coarse sandpaper, and exposed stone: each presents a different shape for the next material to contact. CSP gives project teams a shared visual reference for that shape. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . It does not certify that the concrete is clean, dry, strong, or ready to coat. Those are separate acceptance questions. What the CSP numbers mean ICRI Guideline 310.2R includes benchmark profiles and discusses the capabilities, operating requirements, and limitations of preparation methods used before sealers, coatings, overlays, and repairs ( ICRI 310.2R ). The ICRI system runs from CSP 1 through CSP 10, with the visual texture becoming progressively more aggressive. The number is a comparator, not a recipe. “Diamond grind” and “shot blast” are methods; “CSP 2” or “CSP 4” is an intended surface result. Tool type, media, speed, pressure, concrete hardness, existing finish, operator technique, and repeated passes can change what a method produces. Where the target comes from The target profile should come from the current instructions or specification for the actual material being bonded. A thin sealer, high-build coating, polymer overlay, and repair mortar do not necessarily call for the same texture. The specifier reconciles the material requirement with the existing slab and project constraints. A useful scope says: Mechanically prepare sound concrete to the profile required by Product X’s current data sheet, provisionally CSP __, then verify against ICRI comparator chips and the project acceptance procedure. A weak scope says: Grind floor as needed. The first statement defines the material, reference, provisional target, and verification. The second defines only an activity. How comparison works in the field ICRI’s official R3 guide library lists a field reference for using CSP replica chips ( ICRI R3 Concrete Guides ). The replica chips are tactile and visual comparators. The prepared concrete is compared with the benchmark texture under suitable light and across representative areas. The inspection should include more than the open centre of a room: edges and corners where a different tool was used; high and low areas; dense or soft placements; repaired sections; locations where old coating or adhesive was removed; ramps, drains, coves, and vertical returns; transitions between equipment passes. Photographs are helpful records but can flatten texture and change scale. They should supplement, not replace, the specified on-site comparison. CSP is only one line on the acceptance sheet Acceptance question Why CSP does not answer it Separate check Is the concrete sound? Weak material can still look rough Sounding, visual evaluation, or specified bond testing Is it clean? Oil and dust can remain in a textured surface Inspection and specified cleaning verification Is it dry enough? Roughness does not measure internal moisture Manufacturer-required moisture test Is laitance removed? A rough-looking weak layer may remain locally Inspect and test the prepared substrate Is the profile uniform? One acceptable spot does not represent the room Grid or representative-area inspection Is the surface too rough? More texture is not always better for a thin layer Compare with the product range and film build ACI’s repair guide likewise frames surface preparation within a broader process of concrete evaluation, material selection, application, and quality control ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). Why “rougher is better” fails An unnecessarily aggressive profile can remove sound concrete, expose aggregate, increase repair or material consumption, create high points that show through a thin coating, and complicate edge matching. An insufficient profile can leave a smooth or contaminated surface that does not meet the bonded material’s requirement. The correct target is therefore a range tied to the selected system. If the current data sheet is silent, request written direction from the manufacturer or qualified specifier instead of guessing upward. Turn CSP into an inspection hold point The most useful time to inspect profile is after preparation and cleanup but before primer conceals the surface. Define a hold point in the schedule: Contractor completes the representative prepared area. Dust and debris are removed using the specified method. Project parties compare the surface with the specified reference. Cleanliness, soundness, defects, repairs, and moisture documentation are reviewed separately. Any adjustment is agreed before the full area proceeds or before primer application. For a large or variable slab, establish a benchmark area at the beginning and protect it as a comparison reference. Record the tool setup only as supporting information; accept the resulting surface, not the machine name. Questions to put in a proposal Which layer controls the target CSP? What current manufacturer document states the requirement? Which preparation method is proposed, and what are its limitations here? How will edges, repairs, and difficult access match the field area? Who supplies the comparator chips or other specified verification tool? When is the inspection hold point? What other tests establish cleanliness, soundness, and moisture suitability? What happens if the prepared surface is outside the target? CSP becomes valuable when it connects a material requirement to a field-verifiable result. Used alone, it is just a texture number. Used with condition assessment, cleaning, moisture evaluation, repairs, and documented acceptance, it helps make “properly prepared” something the owner and installer can actually discuss. This overview does not reproduce the ICRI guideline or set a profile for any product. Use the current manufacturer requirement, project specification, and qualified field verification. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Official preparation guide with benchmark concrete surface profiles. ICRI R3 Concrete Guides International Concrete Repair Institute · Official field-guide page listing the guide to using CSP replica chips. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Context for condition evaluation, preparation, repair, and quality control.
