## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/diamond-grinding-concrete-preparation/
Diamond Grinding for Floor Prep | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Diamond grinding uses rotating abrasive segments to remove a controlled layer from concrete. In floor-coating work, its value is not that it makes concrete look scratched. It can remove certain coatings and surface contaminants, open the surface, flatten small projections, and expose defects that were hidden. The required result is a sound, clean, suitably profiled substrate—not a specified number of machine passes. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . What grinding can realistically do Depending on the tooling and concrete, grinding may: remove paint, thin coatings, adhesive residue, laitance, or surface sealer; reduce ridges, trowel marks, and minor high spots; prepare edges and small rooms that larger equipment cannot access; blend patch boundaries; reveal cracks, weak areas, oil penetration, and previous repairs; produce a profile appropriate for some coating or repair materials. ICRI 310.2R summarizes concrete preparation methods by capabilities, operating needs, limitations, and benchmark surface profiles ( ICRI 310.2R ). That source is useful precisely because method selection is not one-size-fits-all. Grinding is not the same as repairing a low slab, diagnosing structural movement, removing deeply absorbed oil, or correcting water vapour. It also does not guarantee the texture required by every coating. The material requirement controls the target. The tooling has to match the layer A project may need different segments for hard concrete, soft concrete, thick coatings, adhesive, or final refinement. Tool selection also changes scratch pattern, removal rate, heat, and the risk of smearing a contaminant instead of removing it. Before full production, prepare a test area that includes the actual existing finish. The test should answer: Does the tooling cut the existing layer cleanly? What concrete profile remains? Is the substrate sound beneath it? Does residue load the tools or spread across the surface? Can edge tooling produce a comparable result? What defects become visible, and how will they be handled? A machine and tooling log can help reproduce the work, but the floor itself remains the acceptance object. Dust control is part of grinding, not cleanup afterward Grinding concrete can generate respirable crystalline silica. Alberta’s current “Silica at the work site” resource points employers to the health effects and legal requirements that apply where silica may be present ( Alberta OHS silica resource ). Alberta’s OHS Code requires employers to minimize release of silica into the air as far as reasonably practicable and keep the work site clear of unnecessary accumulations ( Alberta OHS Code, Part 4 ). An appropriate work plan is developed by competent parties and may include source capture, suitable dust collectors and filters, equipment inspection, restricted access, housekeeping that avoids re-aerosolizing dust, exposure assessment, and required respiratory protection. A household vacuum and open exterior door are not a substitute for that plan. Owners should ask where collected dust goes, how filters and bags are changed, how adjacent equipment is protected, and how the area is released for the next trade. Edges reveal whether the scope is complete Large grinders cannot reach every wall, post, drain, stair, or equipment base. Edge grinders and hand tools behave differently, so an “edge halo”—a smoother or more heavily scratched strip—can remain. The quote should identify: whether baseboards, shelving, or equipment block access; the width and finish standard for perimeter work; details at floor drains, control joints, columns, and thresholds; how vertical returns or coves are prepared; how edge dust is captured; whether inaccessible areas are excluded or require another method. Do not wait until the colour coat to decide what “to the wall” meant. Inspect before the primer hides the evidence Use a hold point after grinding and final cleaning. Walk the floor under strong side lighting and mark: Check Acceptable evidence Existing layer removal No unapproved paint, adhesive, sealer, or soft residue remains Profile Representative areas match the product requirement and specified comparator Soundness Weak, hollow, scaling, or damaged areas are identified for repair Cleanliness Dust and loose abrasive material are removed; no oily smear is visible Uniformity Edges, centres, repairs, and tool transitions meet the same acceptance plan Damage control No unapproved gouges, exposed services, or excessive aggregate removal Defect map Newly visible cracks, spalls, and moisture observations are documented Profile alone does not prove cleanliness, moisture suitability, or bond strength. If the specification requires pull-off testing or another quantitative check, record the method, locations, and acceptance values separately. Grinding versus another method Choose based on the substrate and finish, not equipment preference. Grinding may suit thin-layer removal, edge work, and projects needing controlled abrasion or some flattening. Shot blasting may offer efficient production and a different profile on open areas. Scarifying can remove more material but leaves a more aggressive texture. Multiple methods may be required across one floor. Ask bidders to state what grinding will remove, the intended profile, dust controls, edge plan, repair assumptions, inspection method, and fallback if the test area fails. That turns “diamond grind included” from a vague line item into a verifiable preparation scope. Keep the test-area photographs and preparation record in the closeout file. If a later coating problem is investigated, they show what was removed, what concrete was exposed, and where repairs were made before primer concealed the floor. The record is also useful when a future owner considers recoating or local repair. Concrete grinding presents serious dust, noise, electrical, and equipment hazards. This article is not a work procedure; qualified employers must meet current Alberta requirements and equipment instructions. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Official guide to preparation-method capabilities, limitations, and benchmark profiles. Alberta OHS: Silica at the work site Government of Alberta · Current Alberta workplace resource on silica hazards and applicable legal requirements. Alberta OHS Code: Chemical hazards and harmful substances Government of Alberta · Official legislation covering control of harmful substances, including silica. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/diy-vs-professional-floor-coating/
DIY vs Pro Floor Coating Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A DIY floor coating is not simply the professional version without labour cost. The homeowner becomes the assessor, specifier, equipment operator, material handler, installer, quality-control lead, and repair crew. That can be reasonable on a small, sound, accessible slab with a forgiving finish. It becomes risky as substrate uncertainty, preparation hazards, timing pressure, or appearance expectations rise. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Use this framework before buying material. Score seven project dimensions Give each category 0, 1, or 2 points. Category 0 points 1 point 2 points Existing slab Sound, bare, no unexplained moisture Minor cracks or known coating Spalls, hollow areas, oil, dampness, unknown layers Preparation access Suitable equipment and full access Tight edges or rental learning curve Fixed equipment, stairs, drains, extensive edges Safety control Competent plan and suitable equipment Some controls need arranging Dust/chemical control, ventilation, or PPE is uncertain System complexity One compatible kit with clear instructions Repairs plus several layers Multiple products, broadcasts, coves, joints, or custom details Timing Flexible start and cure period One fixed weekend Hard reopening deadline or cold/variable conditions Appearance tolerance Variation and touch-ups acceptable Uniform colour expected Decorative finish must be consistent across large area Recovery Small area can be redone Rework is disruptive Failure affects operations, stored goods, vehicles, or finished rooms 0–4: DIY may be a reasonable candidate after product and safety review. 5–8: obtain a professional assessment or simplify the scope. 9–14: professional specification and execution are usually the prudent path. The score is a decision prompt, not a guarantee. Preparation is the real dividing line Rolling material is visible and intuitive; diagnosing and preparing concrete is less so. ICRI 310.2R explains that preparation methods differ in capabilities, operating requirements, limitations, and resulting profiles ( ICRI 310.2R ). A DIY plan should be able to answer: What existing material or contaminant must be removed? What surface profile does the exact coating require? How will that profile be verified at the centre and edges? Which cracks are dormant, which lines are joints, and which damage needs evaluation? Which moisture test and acceptance limit apply? How will dust be captured and the floor cleaned without recontamination? What is the fallback if preparation exposes weak or wet concrete? If those questions cannot be answered from current manufacturer documents and a defensible assessment, product shopping is premature. Price the complete DIY job Compare like with like. A DIY budget includes grinder or blaster rental, compatible dust collection, edge tooling, abrasives, power requirements, crack and spall repair, moisture testing, cleaning supplies, mixing tools, spike shoes or squeegees where specified, protective equipment, waste disposal, extra material for the actual profile, and the value of rework. Also budget time for collection, setup, practice, edge work, equipment return, and maintaining cure conditions. A kit’s coverage estimate may assume a substrate and film thickness different from the floor in front of you; use the current product calculation and measured area, not only the label headline. Treat safety as a go/no-go criterion Grinding concrete can release respirable crystalline silica. Alberta’s current silica resource directs work sites to the health effects and applicable legal requirements ( Alberta OHS silica guidance ). Chemical components bring separate hazards and controls. CCOHS explains that a safety data sheet communicates hazards, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, accidental-release measures, and other essential information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). Read the SDS for every component before purchase, including cleaners and repair products. Ensure controls work together; for example, ventilation decisions can affect temperature, dust containment, neighbours, and ignition sources. Do not proceed if you cannot safely operate the preparation equipment, control dust, isolate occupants, handle spills, or manage mixed chemical waste. Hiring only the hazardous preparation stage may be possible, but verify that the prepared surface and timing remain compatible with your later work. Test the hardest square metres first A sample on clean centre-floor concrete proves little. Use a representative area containing an edge, repair, old stain, or other real constraint. Run the entire proposed sequence at small scale and check: removal rate and tool wear; profile and cleanliness; repair appearance; mixing and application pace; working edge and broadcast consistency; cure under actual temperature and ventilation; texture and colour under normal lighting. If the sample fails, change the plan before committing the whole room. Do not bury a preparation problem under a thicker coat unless the manufacturer specifically designs and approves that approach. When professional work adds value Professional involvement is most useful where judgement and recovery matter: unknown old coatings, moisture, extensive repairs, occupied or commercial spaces, short recoat windows, multi-layer systems, decorative broadcast, drainage and cove details, or a hard reopening date. A credible proposal should still expose the method, products, acceptance tests, exclusions, and closeout evidence; “professional” is not itself a specification. You can also split responsibility deliberately: owner clears the room and handles post-cure setup; contractor assesses, prepares, repairs, and installs the system. Put the hand-off condition in writing so neither side assumes the other controls moisture testing, cleaning, or protection. The rational choice is the one that preserves a safe recovery path. If a DIY result can be imperfect without serious consequence and the substrate is understood, learning may be worth it. If failure means removing a bonded system from an occupied or operational floor, the apparent labour saving should be weighed against that downside. This framework is not equipment training or chemical-safety advice. Follow current product labels, SDSs, equipment instructions, and applicable law; use qualified help where hazards or substrate conditions exceed your competence. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Preparation-method capabilities, limitations, and surface-profile verification. Alberta OHS: Silica at the work site Government of Alberta · Official Alberta information about silica hazards and legal requirements at work sites. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Explains SDS purpose, sections, and responsibilities. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/epoxy-floor-odours-ventilation/
Plan Epoxy Odours and Ventilation | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Odour is useful as a complaint—someone is experiencing something in a place—but it is a poor instrument. A strong smell does not quantify exposure, and little or no smell does not prove that a product or work area is safe. Plan an epoxy floor project from the exact products, their safety data, the building’s air pathways, and the people who use the space. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Start with a product inventory, not the word “epoxy” A floor system can include degreaser, crack filler, repair mortar, primer, resin, hardener, colour coat, broadcast aggregate, topcoat, and cleaning solvent. Each may have different hazards and handling controls. Obtain the current Canadian SDS and product data sheet for every component before scheduling. CCOHS explains that SDS sections cover hazard identification, composition, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls and personal protection, physical properties, stability, and disposal, among other information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). Review the complete documents; a VOC figure or “low odour” description is not a replacement. Create a one-page register with product name, component, SDS revision date, quantity, task, work zone, and responsible person. If a product changes, repeat the review. Map how air actually moves Draw the floor and the rooms above, below, and beside it. Mark: supply and return-air grilles; shared corridors, stairwells, elevator shafts, and service chases; exterior doors and operable windows; nearby air intakes, balconies, and neighbouring entrances; exhaust discharge point and replacement-air path; pressure-sensitive rooms; floor drains or penetrations connecting spaces; areas where occupants cannot be relocated. Ventilation is a route, not simply a fan. Exhausting from a basement without intentional replacement air may pull air through the very rooms meant to be protected. Discharging beside an intake or open window can return contaminants to the building. Health Canada recommends reducing or removing pollutant sources, following label instructions, and improving ventilation during activities such as renovation ( Health Canada indoor-air guidance ). A competent project team should translate those principles into equipment, airflow direction, isolation, duration, and monitoring appropriate to the products and site. Separate four access decisions “You can come back tomorrow” is too broad. Establish criteria for: Worker entry during application: based on the hazard assessment, SDS, training, controls, and required PPE. Other-trade entry: based on task compatibility, barriers, exposure controls, and risk of contaminating uncured material. Brief owner inspection: with defined route, authorization, and conditions. Normal occupancy or operations: based on manufacturer cure/use instructions, completed ventilation plan, removal of waste and open containers, and site-specific approval. These moments may occur at different times. “Dry to touch” describes a surface observation, not indoor-air clearance or readiness for normal traffic. VOC, odour, and sensitization are different topics Health Canada describes VOCs as a large group of chemicals present in indoor and outdoor air, with indoor sources including paints, solvents, and other products ( Health Canada VOC guidance ). A product’s VOC content can inform comparison and regulatory classification, but it does not summarize every hazardous ingredient, exposure route, or reaction hazard. Likewise, fragrance intensity varies by chemical and person. Some ingredients can present skin or eye hazards even when vapour is controlled. Review SDS hazard statements, routes of exposure, protective equipment, and first-aid information rather than treating a respirator or open window as a universal solution. A practical pre-start ventilation brief Ask the contractor and building representative to sign off on these items: Topic Decision to document Products Exact components and current SDS/PDS received Isolation Doors, penetrations, HVAC zones, signs, and access control Exhaust Equipment, discharge location, operating period, and contingency Replacement air Source, route, temperature effect, and security Occupants Relocation, notification, vulnerable-person considerations Monitoring Conditions or measurements required by plan; responsible person Waste Mixed material, wipes, containers, and spill supplies Re-entry Separate criteria for workers, inspections, other trades, and occupants Notify affected occupants before odour reaches them. State what work is happening, which spaces are restricted, who receives concerns, and how the plan will change if odour appears outside the expected zone. Do not make medical assurances. If odour travels outside the zone Treat it as evidence that the airflow or isolation assumption may be wrong. Pause work if the site plan requires it, protect people, locate the pathway, check exhaust and replacement air, close open containers, and consult the SDS and responsible safety personnel. Record the time, location, product, task, and corrective action. Do not answer a complaint by saying “it is only the smell.” The appropriate response is to investigate whether controls are operating as designed and whether the hazard assessment still applies. What a responsible proposal says A useful proposal avoids blanket phrases such as “zero fumes” or “completely safe.” It identifies products, attaches safety information, describes isolation and ventilation responsibilities, gives product-specific cure/use criteria, and states that conditions or product substitutions trigger review. It also explains which party controls the building HVAC and who can stop work. Good planning does not promise that nobody will notice an odour. It reduces uncontrolled exposure, prevents air from wandering through occupied areas, and creates a clear response if the building behaves differently from the drawing. This article is general planning information, not an exposure assessment or ventilation design. Qualified parties must use current Canadian SDSs, applicable workplace requirements, and site-specific professional advice. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Health Canada: Volatile organic compounds Health Canada · Official explanation of indoor VOC sources, health effects, and exposure reduction. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Source-control and ventilation guidance for renovations. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Official Canadian guidance to SDS content and use. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/epoxy-flooring-vs-concrete-paint/
Epoxy Flooring vs Concrete Paint | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Concrete paint and epoxy flooring can both add colour to a slab, but the useful comparison is not “paint versus epoxy” as two uniform products. Concrete paints vary by binder and intended use. Epoxy products range from thin water-based coatings to primers, high-build body coats, mortars, and multi-layer broadcast systems. Compare named products and complete scopes. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . The fastest way to separate them Ask for the product data sheet and answer four questions: Is it one component or does it cure after measured components are mixed? What prepared concrete condition and profile does it require? What dry-film thickness or application rate is specified? Is it a standalone finish or one layer in a tested system? A label using “epoxy” as an adjective does not answer those questions. Sika’s official epoxy-coating catalogue, for example, includes binders, primers/sealers, membranes, pigmented finishes, and high-build products rather than one generic epoxy ( Sika epoxy coating catalogue ). This is a bounded illustration of category breadth, not a product recommendation. Side-by-side decision table Topic Typical concrete paint project Multi-part epoxy system project Material Often a ready-to-use architectural coating Resin and hardener mixed in a controlled ratio; may include several layers Working time Usually governed by drying and open time Also limited by mixed-material pot life and recoat windows Film build Commonly a thinner decorative film Can be specified as a higher-build or broadcast system Preparation Cleaning plus whatever abrasion the exact data sheet requires Usually a defined mechanical preparation and profile tied to the system Repairs Minor defects may remain visible Repairs are integrated into the substrate and system scope Application risk Easier to pause and resume on some products Batch timing, mixing, wet edges, and intercoat timing matter Future refresh May be simpler to recoat after compatible preparation May require abrasion, compatibility review, or removal depending on condition Best comparison Product-to-product Complete system-to-complete system These are planning tendencies, not definitions. A premium single-component coating can require demanding preparation, and a thin two-part epoxy is not automatically a heavy-duty flooring system. Preparation remains the common denominator Neither category makes weak, oily, wet, or previously sealed concrete disappear. ICRI 310.2R describes the capabilities and limitations of preparation methods and provides benchmark profiles for coatings, overlays, and repairs ( ICRI 310.2R ). For either option, the quote should state: how old paint, adhesive, curing compound, sealer, and oil are assessed; which mechanical or cleaning method is used; the required surface profile and verification; the moisture test and the product’s acceptance limit; crack, spall, joint, and edge treatment; how dust and debris are removed before application. A lower-cost finish over inadequate preparation is not an equivalent bid. Compare what happens beneath the colour. Decide from service conditions Write a one-year floor diary before selecting material. Include parked vehicles, winter salt and meltwater, tyres, workbench chemicals, rubber mats, rolling loads, sunlight at an open door, cleaning tools, and how often the floor stays wet. Then ask each product supplier for written suitability and limitations for those exposures. A generic “chemical resistant” statement needs the actual chemical, concentration, temperature, contact time, and cleaning method. A generic “garage paint” description needs equal scrutiny regarding tyres, moisture, preparation, and exterior exposure. For Edmonton garages, cold-weather application and salt-laden meltwater are practical design inputs, but no city-wide product choice follows from them. The selected product documents must address the actual slab and operating conditions. VOC language does not define durability Canada’s architectural-coatings regulations set VOC concentration limits across identified coating categories ( ECCC regulatory overview ). VOC content is therefore an environmental and indoor-air planning datum, not a ranking of bond, thickness, wear, chemical resistance, or service life. Review the Canadian SDS for hazards and controls and the product data sheet for installation and performance. “Water-based,” “low VOC,” and “100% solids” each describe only part of a product; none is a complete safety or durability claim. Compare the full owner effort For concrete paint, include cleaning, abrasion, repairs, primer if required, coats, protection, and future refresh. For epoxy flooring, include mechanical preparation, dust control, moisture testing, repairs, all system layers, environment control, restricted cure, and maintenance. Ask both options for the same closeout information: exact product and colour identifiers; batch or lot records; preparation and moisture documentation; installation conditions; maintenance instructions; leftover touch-up material and its shelf/storage limits; written exclusions and repair procedure. The simplest decision rule is this: choose concrete paint when a refreshable decorative finish matches the slab, use, preparation commitment, and appearance tolerance. Consider a specified epoxy system when the added film build, texture, design, or exposure performance is justified—and when the site can support the more controlled preparation and application sequence. Do not compare a can of paint with a professionally installed multi-layer system by price per square metre. Compare two defined scopes against the same floor diary, then decide whether the added system complexity solves a problem you actually have. If the choice remains close, coat two representative test areas rather than relying on loose colour chips. Include an edge and a repaired or stained section. Evaluate coverage, texture, defect visibility, application pace, and cleaning after the manufacturer permits service. A sample cannot predict service life, but it can expose false assumptions about appearance and labour. This article is general product-selection guidance. Confirm compatibility, application conditions, safety controls, and service suitability in current Canadian manufacturer documents for every named product. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ECCC: VOC Concentration Limits for Architectural Coatings Regulations Environment and Climate Change Canada · Official overview of Canadian VOC limits for architectural-coating categories. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Concrete preparation methods, limitations, and benchmark profiles. Sikafloor epoxy coatings Sika Corporation · Bounded manufacturer example illustrating the variety of epoxy binders, primers, membranes, and coatings. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/flake-vs-metallic-vs-solid-epoxy/
Flake vs Metallic vs Solid Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor The quick comparison Flake is the practical choice for most garages. A base coat, a broadcast of coloured flake, a scrape, and a clear top coat make a textured, speckled floor that hides dust, grit, and small scratches. Solid colour is one even colour under a top coat. It looks clean and architectural and brightens a room, but it shows dust, tire marks, and scratches sooner. Metallic is poured and worked by hand so metallic pigments settle into swirls and depth. No two floors are alike. It is the most decorative of the three and the least forgiving of dust and wear. All three are epoxy systems on prepared concrete. The preparation underneath follows the same idea for each, because the prepared surface has to suit the coating, as the ICRI guideline on surface preparation sets out. What changes is what you see, and how the floor lives with daily use. How each one looks Flake reads as texture from across the room and as colour up close. The colour comes from the blend, a mix of tones and chip sizes. Full coverage, where flake covers the whole base, gives a granite-like surface. Partial coverage lets the base colour show between the chips. Our flake colour guide covers how blends read in different light. Solid colour is calm. Greys, charcoals, and light neutrals are common in garages and workshops. A light solid floor bounces light around and makes a room feel bigger. Metallic floors have movement. Light travels through the pigments, so the floor looks different at noon and at night. That depth is the appeal, and the variation is part of it: the final pattern is shaped by the pour and cannot be predicted exactly. Read the metallic expectations guide before choosing one. What each one hides, and what it shows This is where most people decide. Dust and grit. Flake hides them best. Solid and metallic floors show a film of dust sooner, especially in dark colours. Scratches. Every coated floor scratches under grit and dragged equipment. Flake disguises fine scratches in its pattern. Solid and metallic floors show them in raking light. Tire marks. Hot tires can mark any coating, and the marks are easiest to see on light solid colours. The hot-tire pickup guide explains the causes. Salt rings. Edmonton winters bring meltwater and road salt into garages. The white rings it leaves when it dries show on dark solid and metallic floors. A mid-tone flake blend hides them. Grip underfoot A smooth, glossy floor can be slippery when wet, whatever its colour. Flake adds a little texture on its own. For any of the three, an anti-slip top coat adds grip where people walk in wet boots or where water sits. The CCOHS guidance on preventing slips, trips, and falls is written for workplaces, and it names the quality of the walking surface as a key factor. The same holds in a garage or a mudroom. Our slip resistance guide goes into texture and top coats. Which finish suits which room Garage. Flake, usually. It handles grit, salt, and daily parking, and still looks good between cleanings. Basement living space. Metallic or solid, where the floor is seen more and dragged on less. See the basement guide . Workshop. A light solid colour for brightness, or flake for forgiveness. Grip where oil or water is around. Showroom or commercial space. Solid colour for a clean, even look, or metallic for a feature area. The solid-colour commercial guide covers commercial choices. Mudroom. Flake with grip, because boots and water arrive together. Time on the floor, and what it means for the quote The preparation underneath is the same idea for all three, so the differences come from the layers on top. Flake has a rhythm: base coat, broadcast, scrape, top coat. The broadcast is fast, and the scrape and top coat make the surface even. Solid colour goes down in rolled or squeegeed coats. It is the simplest to install, and the least forgiving of a poorly prepared slab, because every flaw in the concrete shows through an even colour. Metallic is poured and worked by hand while it is wet, so it takes the most skilled time on the floor. The look depends on that hand work, which is why two metallic floors never match. Those differences show up in time and in the quote. Ask for the options side by side so you compare like with like; the guide to garage coating costs explains the other factors. Colour and light in an Edmonton garage Garage light changes the colour you chose. Winter daylight is low and blue, and most garage lighting is cool LED. Warm greys can look flat under cool light, and very dark floors swallow light in a single-bulb garage. Before choosing, look at colours in your own space at the time of day you use it most. A light or mid-tone floor makes a garage brighter to work in, and hides salt rings better than black. Living with each one All three clean the same way: a dust mop or soft broom, then a damp mop with a mild cleaner. The difference is how often you notice the need. Flake forgives a busy week. Solid and metallic floors look their best with more frequent dust mopping. The cleaning guide has the details. See it before you choose Colour on a screen is a starting point. The finish library shows the flake, solid, and metallic families, and the floor visualizer lets you try them on a photo of your own space. When you have a direction, ask Denis what suits your floor. Final Finish installs flake, metallic, and decorative epoxy floors in Edmonton; see residential epoxy flooring for the service. Questions people ask Which epoxy finish is best for a garage in Edmonton? For most garages, flake. Its texture and speckled colour hide grit, salt residue, and fine scratches between cleanings, and it gives a little grip underfoot. Solid colour and metallic floors suit rooms that see less winter traffic. Is a metallic epoxy floor slippery? A smooth, glossy metallic floor can be slippery when wet, like any glossy surface. Where water or snow comes in, an anti-slip top coat adds grip. In dry living spaces, most people keep the smooth finish. Do scratches show on a solid colour epoxy floor? More than on flake. Every coated floor scratches under grit and dragged equipment, but a flake pattern disguises fine scratches, while a solid colour shows them in low, raking light. Dust mopping and felt pads help. Can I see the finishes on my own floor before choosing? The floor visualizer on this site lets you try finish families on a photo of your own space. Colour on a screen is a starting point, so talk through the choice with Denis before the quote. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading CCOHS: Prevention of slips, trips and falls Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Walking surfaces, housekeeping, and footwear in slip and fall prevention. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-contractor-checklist/
Floor Coating Contractor Checks | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Use this checklist to make bids comparable. It does not tell you which contractor to hire; it reveals whether each contractor has priced the same floor, preparation, system, safety obligations, and hand-off. For local scope options, see our commercial epoxy flooring . Before inviting bids Write the room use, traffic, chemicals, cleaning method, wet conditions, texture priorities, and appearance expectations. Mark cracks, joints, spalls, drains, slopes, edges, old coatings, oil, damp areas, and fixed equipment on a floor plan. State access hours, available power, water, heating, ventilation control, storage, and waste restrictions. Identify the owner representative who can approve hidden-condition changes. Give every bidder the same photos, floor plan, service conditions, and required bid format. Do not begin with a desired resin name alone. A product can only be evaluated against the substrate and use. Contractor and project administration Legal business name and contact information appear on the proposal. The proposal identifies who supervises the work and who performs specialized testing. Required licensing, insurance, permits, and workplace documentation are verified for the actual project—not assumed from a logo. Subcontracted preparation, testing, repairs, electrical work, or waste handling is disclosed. The owner and contractor roles for clearing, utilities, HVAC, security, shutdowns, and emergency access are explicit. Change authorization requires a written scope, price or method, and schedule effect. For commercial projects, consult the official Alberta OHS Act, Regulation, and Code and assign project responsibilities with competent advice ( Alberta OHS legislation ). Do not treat this website checklist as a compliance review. Assessment and preparation scope Concrete condition is assessed across representative areas, including edges and beneath movable items. Existing coatings, adhesives, sealers, curing compounds, and contamination are identified or listed as unknowns. Moisture method, locations, timing, results, and product acceptance limits are stated. Crack, spall, weak-concrete, joint, and repair treatment is itemized. The mechanical preparation method and target surface profile are named. Edges, drains, stairs, columns, coves, thresholds, and inaccessible areas have a defined detail. Dust collection, isolation, cleanup, and prepared-surface inspection are included. A hold point occurs after preparation and before primer. ICRI 310.2R explains that preparation methods have different capabilities, operating requirements, limitations, and resulting profiles ( ICRI 310.2R ). “Diamond grind as needed” is therefore less useful than a method, target, edge plan, and verification procedure. Materials and system build Every layer is named by manufacturer and product: repair, primer, body coat, aggregate or flake, grout coat, and topcoat. Colour, sheen, broadcast density, texture, and sample or mock-up approval are documented. Coverage or thickness is stated in the manufacturer’s applicable terms. Product substitutions require written owner approval and renewed compatibility review. Current product data sheets and Canadian SDSs are attached. The contractor states which document governs moisture, temperature, humidity, dew point, mixing, pot life, recoat, and cure. Treatment at intentional joints and moving cracks is explicit. Chemical, UV, tyre, impact, and slip claims are tied to written product/system data and actual use. CCOHS explains that SDSs communicate hazard identification, first aid, accidental-release measures, handling, exposure controls, properties, and other essential information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). An SDS addresses safety; it does not replace the product data sheet or system specification. Site logistics and safety coordination Work-zone barriers, signs, authorized access, and adjacent occupant notification are planned. Dust, odour, noise, electrical loads, cords, hoses, and waste routes are addressed. HVAC isolation, exhaust discharge, and replacement-air paths are agreed with the building representative. Material delivery, heated or secure storage, spill response, and mixed-product disposal are assigned. Other trades and live operations are coordinated. Emergency exits, fire equipment, panels, shutoffs, and drains remain appropriately accessible. Contingencies cover power loss, unsuitable conditions, unexpected moisture, and hidden deterioration. The contractor’s safe-work plan should fit the actual site. Do not ask for a generic template merely to tick a box; ask who reviewed it after the site walk. Schedule and inspection gates The schedule separates clearing, preparation, repairs, layers, restricted cure, and recommissioning. Product-specific minimum and maximum recoat windows are mapped to shifts. Required air, slab, material, humidity, and condensation conditions are logged. There are named stop/go decisions before repair concealment, primer, each layer, traffic, and reopening. Traffic classes are separate: worker access, owner inspection, foot traffic, equipment, vehicles, washing, and normal service. Delays caused by conditions have a written decision path. Reject generic phrases such as “ready next day” unless the bid states ready for what, under which measured conditions, and according to which product document. Commercial terms and exclusions Tax, mobilization, equipment moves, utilities, protection, waste, and cleanup are included or clearly excluded. Repair quantity and the unit rate or allowance for concealed damage are stated. Payment milestones follow observable deliverables. Warranty language identifies the provider, duration, covered defects, exclusions, maintenance duties, and claim process. No promise depends on an unverified assumption such as a dry slab or intact vapour retarder. Cancellation, delay, and owner-caused access changes are addressed. Do not infer credentials, warranties, or performance from marketing language. Verify documents directly and keep copies with the signed agreement. Closeout package Final product names, colours, lots, and SDS/PDS versions are supplied. Moisture, preparation, repair, environmental, batch, and inspection records are delivered. Photographs show the prepared floor and concealed repairs. Cleaning products, routine, prohibited practices, and inspection intervals are written. Spare material is labelled with storage and shelf-life instructions, if supplied. Punch-list items and accepted appearance variations are recorded. Reopening authorization identifies permitted use and date/time. Score each bid as clear , assumption , or missing beside every applicable item. Clarify assumptions before comparing price. The strongest proposal is not necessarily the longest; it is the one that turns important decisions into verifiable scope and leaves little room for two parties to imagine different floors. This checklist is general procurement guidance, not legal, engineering, insurance, or occupational-health advice. Verify requirements and documents with qualified Alberta professionals. Commercial epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta OHS Act, Regulation and Code Government of Alberta · Official access to Alberta workplace health and safety legislation. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Canadian guidance on SDS content and use. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Preparation methods, limitations, and benchmark profiles. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-estimate-from-photos/
Floor Coating Estimate by Photo | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Can you get a floor coating estimate from photos? Yes. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, and for most garages and basements, good photos get most of the way to a real number. The photos have to show what drives the price: the size and shape of the floor, the condition of the concrete, the damage, and anything the coating has to work around. Here is what to send, how to take it, and what no photo can tell anyone. Start with the whole floor Clear what you can, even if only for the photos. A floor hidden under storage bins cannot be judged. Then take four wide shots: Two corner shots. Stand in one corner and photograph the floor to the far corner. Then do the opposite corner. Together they show the whole slab. From the doorway. For a garage, stand outside the open overhead door and shoot in. This shows the door strip, the parking tracks, and the slope toward the door or drain. From the back wall. Turn around and shoot toward the door. Shoot in daylight with the lights on. Avoid a flash pointed straight at the floor; it flattens texture and hides stains. Then the close-ups Close-ups show what the preparation and repairs will involve: Cracks. One wide shot to show where they run, then a close-up with a coin or a tape measure beside the widest point for scale. Stains. Oil under the engine bay, rust marks, and anything dark or shiny. Edges and damage. Chips at the door, broken edges, and spots where salt has scaled the surface. Old finishes. Paint, a sealer, or an old coating, especially where it is peeling. A close-up of a lifting edge says more than a paragraph. Drains, steps, and posts. Anything the coating has to stop at or wrap around. Signs of water. White powdery deposits, damp corners, or water marks along a wall. Add the numbers and the story Photos show the condition. A few facts fill in the rest: Rough measurements, wall to wall. How the space is used: parking, a workshop, a home gym, storage, or living space. Whether the space is heated, and whether the slab has in-floor heat. Any history of water, and whether the slab is new. The finish you are leaning toward. The finish library and the floor visualizer help if you are not sure yet. When you would like the floor done. A short video works too. Walk slowly, keep the floor in frame, and say what you know about it. What photos cannot show Photos show the surface. They do not show what is inside the slab. Three things usually need someone on site: Moisture. Moisture in concrete is measured, not seen. ASTM F2170 describes testing relative humidity inside the slab. A dry-looking floor in a photo does not rule it out. The bond of old coatings. Paint or an old coating can look sound and still come up in sheets once grinding starts. Hollow or weak concrete. Delaminated areas sound different when tapped. A camera cannot hear them. That is why an estimate from photos is a starting point for the scope, not a promise about every square metre. The surface preparation has to suit the coating system, as the ICRI guideline on surface preparation sets out, and some of that can only be confirmed on the floor. Photo mistakes that slow an estimate Most back-and-forth comes from a handful of habits: Only close-ups. A tight shot of a crack says nothing about where it runs or how much floor there is. Always send the wide shots first. No scale. A crack can look like a hairline or a canyon depending on the zoom. Put a coin, a pen, or a tape measure beside it. A covered floor. Bins, mats, and a parked car hide exactly what matters. Move what you can, even to one side. Night light. Warm bulbs turn grey concrete yellow and hide stains. Daylight through the open door is best for a garage. Blurry phones. Tap the screen to focus on the floor, hold still, and take two of each shot. When a visit is the better start Photos work well for most garages and basements. A visit is often the better first step when the floor is large or commercial, when there is a known water problem, when an old coating is peeling in patches, or when a new slab may have been sealed and nobody knows with what. It also helps when the space is hard to photograph, such as a long shop with poor light. You can ask for either; the estimate is free both ways. What a good estimate tells you back Whatever you send, the reply should be specific: the preparation the floor needs, which repairs are included, the system and finish proposed, what is not included, and what could change once the floor is ground. Alberta’s advice on hiring a contractor is to get estimates and changes in writing. Our guide to garage coating costs explains what moves the number, and the contractor questions guide lists what to ask next. Send them to Denis When the photos are ready, send them through the quote form or call (780) 991-1651. Say what the space is for and when you would like the floor done. You will hear what the photos show, and whether a visit would help before a firm quote. More on the work itself: residential epoxy flooring and commercial epoxy flooring . Questions people ask How many photos should I send for a floor coating estimate? Usually eight to twelve: two corner shots of the whole floor, one from the doorway, one from the back wall, and close-ups of cracks, stains, damaged edges, drains, and any old coating. A slow video walk-around can replace some of them. Do I need exact measurements? No. Rough wall-to-wall measurements are enough to start. Note anything that breaks the floor up, such as a step, a drain, or a curb, because edges and details take more time than open floor. Is an estimate from photos the final price? It is a starting point for the scope. Moisture, the bond of an old coating, and hollow concrete cannot be judged from a picture. Ask what the estimate assumes and what could change once the floor is ground or tested. Is the estimate free? Yes. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, for garages, basements, shops, and commercial floors in Edmonton. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Hiring a contractor Government of Alberta · Consumer guidance on written estimates, contracts, and changes. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Standard test for relative humidity inside a concrete slab. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-recoat-windows/
Why Floor Recoat Timing Matters | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A recoat window is the period in which one layer may receive the next layer under the manufacturer’s stated conditions and preparation. It has two edges: too early and too late. “Apply tomorrow” is not a recoat specification because temperature, product, layer thickness, humidity, and the condition of the first coat can change the permitted timing. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Minimum and maximum solve different problems The minimum wait helps ensure the first layer has progressed far enough to accept the next operation without unacceptable disturbance, solvent entrapment, marking, or other product-specific problems. The maximum wait marks the point beyond which the manufacturer may require additional cleaning, abrasion, primer, or another procedure to establish intercoat bond. The exact reason and remedy depend on the chemistry and system. Do not confuse these times: pot life: usable time after components are mixed; working time: practical application period; tack-free or dry-to-touch time; recoat window; foot-traffic time; vehicle or equipment traffic time; full cure or chemical-service time. They may appear on the same data sheet but govern different decisions. Why a universal number is impossible As one bounded example, Sikafloor-217 publishes different minimum and maximum recoat times at 10°C, 20°C, and 30°C, alongside separate pot-life and traffic times ( Sikafloor-217 data ). A second Sika product, Sikafloor-7500, publishes a different set of waiting periods and also lists ambient, substrate, humidity, and condensation conditions ( Sikafloor-7500 data ). These examples are not recommendations for an Edmonton project. They demonstrate that even one manufacturer’s epoxy products do not share a single “epoxy recoat time.” Use the Canadian documents and written system instructions for the products actually supplied. Build a layer-by-layer timing matrix Do this before mobilization, not after the first coat is down. From → to Product documents Site conditions used Earliest start Latest start If missed Repair → primer Repair and primer PDS Slab/air/material values Calculated time Calculated time Written repair/primer procedure Primer → body coat Both layer documents Recorded conditions Calculated time Calculated time Clean/abrade/reprime as directed Body coat → grout/topcoat System and layer documents Recorded conditions Calculated time Calculated time Manufacturer-approved recovery Topcoat → traffic Topcoat document Recorded cure conditions By traffic class Not applicable Extend restriction/reassess Use actual dates and clock times. If a layer begins at 3:40 p.m., a 24-hour maximum is not “sometime the next day.” Add shift changes, inspection, masking, broadcast removal, cleaning, and condition verification before the deadline. Conditions belong beside the clock Record air temperature, slab temperature, material temperature where required, relative humidity, and condensation margin at the locations and frequency specified for the system. A cold edge beside an overhead door may cure differently from the centre. Averaging conditions across the room can hide the limiting area. Also log: product, component, lot, and batch; mixing and placement start/finish; area or zone; film or broadcast checks required by the specification; observed contamination, blush, tack, or damage; inspection and authorization for the next layer. The record makes a later decision traceable. Without it, “we were within the window” is only a recollection. A missed window is a technical decision Stop and protect the floor. Do not automatically place the next coat, and do not invent a sanding routine. Gather the layer product, elapsed time, actual conditions, surface observations, and current documents. Then obtain the manufacturer’s written recovery procedure where the data sheet does not already give one. A recovery may require washing, cleaning, mechanical abrasion to a defined result, dust removal, solvent wiping where specifically permitted, a new primer, or removal and replacement. The correct sequence depends on the product and the contamination or cure state. After recovery, inspect the whole affected zone, including edges and areas that received the earlier coat at different times. Document the deviation, instruction received, work performed, and revised next-layer window. Protect the first coat while waiting “Waiting” is an active site condition. Restrict foot traffic and other trades. Prevent dust, insects, water, condensation, oil, overspray, cleaning residue, and heater exhaust from reaching the layer. Plan how broadcast aggregate is collected without contaminating adjacent uncured work. If the space is occupied or products present chemical hazards, maintain the ventilation and access controls required by the hazard assessment. CCOHS explains that SDSs contain handling, storage, exposure-control, accidental-release, and other safety information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). Cure timing does not cancel those requirements. Schedule backwards from the hardest boundary The hardest boundary is often a maximum recoat time, a building shutdown, or the earliest permitted return to a particular traffic class. Work backwards to set batch times, inspection shifts, environmental control, and contingency. For multi-zone projects, use a zone map and separate clock for each placement. Staggering may make labour manageable, but it multiplies deadlines. Assign one person to maintain the live matrix and authorize layer transitions. A credible proposal states the exact products, provisional windows at planned conditions, monitoring method, overnight controls, and missed-window procedure. That is the difference between a schedule built from chemistry and a schedule built from hope. Product data governs. This guide does not establish any recoat or traffic time. Use current Canadian PDSs and SDSs, recorded site conditions, and written manufacturer direction. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Sikafloor-217 product data Sika Corporation · Bounded example with temperature-dependent pot life, cure, and recoat ranges. Sikafloor-7500 product data Sika Corporation · Second bounded example showing different recoat ranges and conditions. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Canadian guidance on obtaining and using current SDS information. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-site-assessment-checklist/
Floor Coating Site Assessment | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A productive site assessment is a fact-finding walk, not a colour consultation. Its goal is to leave with a floor plan, condition map, service brief, testing plan, logistics constraints, and a list of unresolved questions. Use this checklist to prepare the space and record what the assessor actually sees. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . Bring before the walk Dimensioned floor plan or a sketch with overall measurements. Construction year and slab drawings, if available. History of previous flooring, coatings, adhesive removal, repairs, leaks, flooding, and drainage work. Product names for cleaners, degreasers, chemicals, and processes that contact the floor. Photos taken during wet events, even if the floor is dry today. Operating schedule, shutdown limits, and equipment-move constraints. Owner priorities ranked: appearance, texture, cleanability, downtime, repairability, exposure, or budget. Do not clean away every clue just before the visit. Remove loose items and obvious trip hazards, but preserve photographs and records of recurring stains, damp areas, and damage. A. What the floor must do Identify pedestrians, footwear, carts, tyres, pallet jacks, forklifts, workbenches, shelving, and point loads. Record wet processes, tracked snow, salt, oils, fuels, food, acids, solvents, disinfectants, or hot materials. Name the cleaning tools, products, water temperature, frequency, and whether liquids pond. Mark sunlight, open overhead doors, exterior transitions, radiant heat, freezers, ovens, or temperature cycling. State desired colour, sheen, texture, line marking, cove, and decorative variation. Decide which scratches, stains, patches, and colour variation would be acceptable. Avoid the word “chemical-resistant” without a chemical list. Exposure duration, concentration, temperature, and cleanup determine what evidence the system supplier should provide. B. Divide the slab into zones Number rooms or production cells and mark boundaries that may indicate different placements. For each zone, photograph and map: cracks, including width, length, edge offset, water, and previous fill; control, construction, isolation, and unknown joints; spalls, scaling, pop-outs, hollow areas, and weak edges; oil, tyre marks, adhesive, paint, curing compound, and suspected sealer; patches and areas with different colour, hardness, or aggregate; slopes, drains, trenches, low areas, ramps, stairs, and thresholds; wall-floor joints, columns, equipment pads, anchors, and penetrations; areas hidden by fixed equipment or inaccessible during the walk. ACI’s concrete-repair guide places condition evaluation before repair strategy, material selection, preparation, application, and quality control ( ACI PRC-546-23 ). The assessment should therefore distinguish observed defects from the repair recommendation that comes later. Mark “unknown” where the floor cannot be seen. The proposal can then price access, exploratory preparation, an allowance, or an approval process rather than inventing certainty. C. Moisture and water history Ask about roof, wall, plumbing, drain, sump, washdown, and groundwater events separately. Mark mineral deposits, damp joints, dark patches, blistered old coatings, and areas beneath mats or storage. Record whether a below-slab vapour retarder is documented, absent, or unknown. Note recent removal of flooring or coatings and whether HVAC is at normal service conditions. Define the moisture test method, number and distribution of locations, timing, and reporting. Obtain the exact coating system’s published acceptance limit before interpreting results. ASTM F2170 is a quantitative method for measuring relative humidity within a concrete slab, and its official significance statement notes that the result represents the slab condition at the time of the test ( ASTM F2170-19a ). A handheld scan, plastic sheet, and in-situ RH probe are not interchangeable simply because all relate to moisture. Visible water entry is a different problem from a coating-acceptance test. Refer unresolved leakage or drainage to the appropriate qualified party. D. Preparation feasibility Identify the likely existing layer and obtain records or plan a test area. Confirm whether large grinders or blasting equipment can reach the floor. Check door width, elevator capacity, stairs, floor loading, and overhead clearance. Locate suitable power, including voltage, phase, amperage, and panel access. Plan dust collection, edge tooling, cleanup, and waste movement. Identify noise, vibration, and dust-sensitive neighbours or processes. Select a representative test area with real coating, edge, repair, or contamination. Define the target profile and how it will be verified before primer. The test area is not a free sample of final colour. It is a controlled way to learn removal rate, tool behaviour, substrate condition, edge quality, and hidden damage before a production schedule is locked. E. Building and operational logistics Measure entrances and identify a material route that does not cross live operations. Assign secure, temperature-appropriate material storage. Mark HVAC supplies, returns, exhausts, intakes, windows, and neighbouring entrances. Identify fire exits, panels, shutoffs, drains, and equipment that must remain accessible. Plan barriers, signs, security, worker facilities, spill response, and waste storage. List other contractors or employees working nearby. Separate reopening needs for inspection, foot traffic, carts, equipment, vehicles, washing, and normal service. For Alberta workplaces, project parties should review responsibilities and applicable requirements through the official OHS Act, Regulation, and Code portal ( Alberta OHS legislation ). A site assessment should flag coordination needs; it is not itself the employer’s hazard assessment or safe-work plan. F. Questions the assessment must leave answered By the end of the visit, require a short findings record: What substrate conditions were observed, and where? Which areas were inaccessible or remain uncertain? Which tests or exploratory work are required before a firm specification? What preparation method and provisional profile are proposed? What repairs are included, allowed for, or excluded? Which exact system layers are candidates, and what use data supports them? What access, environmental, ventilation, and shutdown controls shape the schedule? Which decisions require an engineer, building specialist, hygienist, manufacturer, or owner? Turn observations into bid attachments Issue the floor plan, defect map, photos, service brief, test results, site constraints, and unanswered questions to every bidder. Ask them to return the same layer schedule, preparation standard, repair quantities, assumptions, exclusions, and closeout documents. An assessment has succeeded when it reduces hidden assumptions. It may conclude that the floor is ready for a defined proposal, that testing or exploratory work comes first, or that water or structural evaluation takes priority. All three are useful outcomes. This checklist is general planning information. Structural conditions, hazardous materials, water entry, exposure controls, and product specification require competent site-specific evaluation. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete evaluation, repair strategy, preparation, application, and quality-control context. ASTM F2170-19a: Relative Humidity in Concrete Floor Slabs ASTM International · Official in-situ relative-humidity test method and limitations. Alberta OHS Act, Regulation and Code Government of Alberta · Official access to current Alberta workplace health and safety legislation. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-terminology-glossary/
Floor Coating Terminology Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Flooring terms often collapse a detailed requirement into one word. Use this glossary to expand the shorthand, then ask which product, test method, condition, or acceptance value applies to your project. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Substrate and preparation Abrasion: Mechanical wearing of a surface. In preparation, abrasion may remove a layer and create texture; the scope should name the method and required result. Bond-inhibiting contaminant: Material such as oil, dust, curing compound, adhesive, wax, or incompatible sealer that can interfere with adhesion. Identification and removal must be method-specific. Concrete surface profile (CSP): ICRI’s visual and tactile scale for comparing prepared-concrete roughness. ICRI 310.2R provides benchmark profiles and describes preparation methods and limitations ( ICRI 310.2R ). CSP does not by itself prove cleanliness, soundness, or moisture suitability. Diamond grinding: Preparation using rotating diamond tooling. It may remove coatings, laitance, or high spots and leave a particular profile, depending on tools, concrete, and technique. Laitance: A weak, fine surface layer on concrete. If present, it is removed to reach sound concrete rather than used as the bonding surface. Mechanical preparation: Use of equipment such as grinders, shot blasters, or scarifiers to remove material and create the specified substrate condition. The equipment name is not an acceptance criterion. Scarifying: Rotary cutting with flails or cutters that removes concrete and leaves an aggressive texture. It is distinct from grinding and may require later refinement. Shot blasting: Propelling and recovering abrasive shot in a contained machine to clean and profile concrete. Edges and inaccessible areas need separate detailing. Sound concrete: Concrete capable of supporting the intended repair or coating. “Looks solid” is not a defined test; the specification should state how soundness is assessed where it matters. Cracks, joints, and repairs Control or contraction joint: An intentional weakened plane intended to manage shrinkage cracking. The flooring detail should say whether it remains active, is filled, or is carried through. Construction joint: Interface between separate concrete placements. It may require a different detail from a random crack. Crack chasing: Cutting or opening a crack to a controlled geometry for a selected repair. It does not diagnose why the crack formed or whether it moves. Delamination: Separation within concrete or between layers. A surface can remain in place while sounding hollow or lacking reliable support. Feather edge: A repair tapering to nearly zero thickness. Many repair products prohibit it; use the manufacturer’s permitted edge detail. Isolation or expansion joint: A joint designed to accommodate movement between elements. Rigidly bridging it can defeat the intended detail. Repair mortar: Material used to replace removed or missing concrete. Select it by repair geometry, service, substrate, cure, and compatibility—not strength number alone. Spall: Localized concrete loss, usually deeper than superficial scaling. The full weak boundary may extend beyond the visible hole. Moisture and environment Dew point: The temperature at which air reaches saturation and condensation can form. Coating data often require the substrate to remain a stated margin above it; use the product’s actual instruction. In-situ relative humidity: Percent relative humidity measured within a concrete slab using probes under ASTM F2170. ASTM notes the result represents the slab condition at the time of testing ( ASTM F2170-19a ). Moisture mitigation: A named system intended to manage slab moisture under defined conditions. It is not a universal cure for water entry or a substitute for testing. Moisture vapour emission rate (MVER): A result from a specified emission test, not another name for internal relative humidity or a handheld meter reading. Relative humidity (air): Amount of water vapour in air relative to the maximum possible at that temperature. Distinguish ambient RH from in-slab RH. Vapour retarder: Material intended to limit vapour transmission within a building assembly. For an existing slab, its presence and condition may be unknown unless construction records establish them. Products and system build Binder: Film-forming portion that holds a coating together and bonds it within its intended system. Broadcast: Aggregate, quartz, or flake distributed into a wet layer. “Full broadcast” still needs a product quantity, rejection point, and finished texture standard. Body coat: Main resinous layer providing much of the system build or encapsulating broadcast material. Dry-film thickness (DFT): Thickness after a coating has cured or dried. It differs from wet-film thickness and theoretical coverage. Epoxy: A class of thermosetting resin systems commonly formed by mixing resin and hardener. The word alone says nothing certain about thickness, UV behaviour, cure, or suitability. High-build: Relative product description indicating a thicker applied film than conventional thin coatings. Require a numeric specified thickness. Primer: First system layer selected to interact with the prepared substrate and later coat. It does not replace preparation unless the system explicitly says so. Resinous flooring system: Compatible sequence of repair, primer, resin, aggregate, body coat, grout coat, and/or topcoat. Not every project uses every layer. Solids content: Portion remaining after volatile components leave, expressed according to the manufacturer’s stated basis. It is not a complete performance or safety rating. Topcoat: Final resinous layer selected for surface properties such as finish, texture, cleanability, light stability, or exposure within a documented system. Wet-film thickness (WFT): Thickness immediately after application. Some liquid coatings use WFT checks as installation quality control. Application and cure Cure: Chemical or physical progression by which material develops intended properties. Cure rate depends on product and conditions; dry-to-touch is not full cure. Induction time: Manufacturer-specified wait after mixing before application for certain products. Never assume one exists or omit it; follow the data sheet. Mix ratio: Required proportion of components by volume or weight. Container sizes do not authorize casual partial batching. Open time: Period during which a layer or adhesive remains able to receive the intended operation under stated conditions. Manufacturers may use this term differently, so verify the definition. Pot life: Time mixed material remains usable under specified conditions. Material in a pail may behave differently from material spread on a floor; follow product instructions. Recoat window: Minimum-to-maximum interval for applying a subsequent layer under stated preparation and conditions. A missed maximum can require a documented recovery procedure. Return to service: Point when a defined use is permitted. Foot traffic, vehicles, washing, chemical exposure, and full cure may have separate times. Wet edge: Fresh boundary maintained so adjacent material blends during application. Crew size, batch planning, and room geometry influence it. Documents and verification Mock-up: Representative installed sample used to agree on appearance, texture, edge detail, or execution standard. A small sample on perfect concrete may not represent the floor. Product data sheet (PDS/TDS): Manufacturer’s technical document covering uses, limits, preparation, mixing, application, and performance data for a product. Confirm revision and region. Safety data sheet (SDS): Standardized hazard-communication document. CCOHS explains its sixteen sections, including hazards, first aid, handling, exposure controls, and disposal information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). It is not a durability specification. Specification: Written requirements for products, execution, testing, acceptance, and closeout. A brand list without preparation and inspection is incomplete. Submittal: Documents provided for review befo

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/floor-coating-voc-basics/
VOC Basics for Floor Coatings | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor VOC means volatile organic compound. In a floor-coating decision, a VOC number can help compare a defined environmental property of products when the calculation basis and category match. It cannot by itself tell you whether the coating is odourless, non-toxic, safe for immediate occupancy, durable, or appropriate for a particular slab. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . What “volatile” describes Health Canada describes VOCs as a large group of chemicals present in indoor and outdoor air and identifies products such as paints and solvents among indoor sources ( Health Canada VOC guidance ). “Volatile” concerns a substance’s tendency to enter the air; it is not a complete hazard ranking. Different VOCs have different health effects, odour thresholds, and exposure limits. A floor system may also contain important non-VOC hazards, including ingredients that affect skin or eyes. That is why VOC content, hazard communication, ventilation, and floor performance remain separate review tracks. Decode the number before comparing it A product may publish VOC content in grams per litre, but comparisons can still fail if one value is: for a single component rather than the mixed product; calculated with or without water and exempt compounds; measured under a different test or regulatory definition; reported for a tint base rather than the finished colour; based on a different regional formulation; for one layer while another proposal reports a complete system. Ask the supplier for the current Canadian technical document and the exact basis of the number. Compare primer with primer, topcoat with topcoat, and whole system with whole system. Environment and Climate Change Canada states that the federal Architectural Coatings Regulations establish VOC concentration limits for identified coating categories ( ECCC regulatory overview ). Regulatory compliance is a minimum legal question for an applicable category; it is not a claim that two compliant products have equal indoor-air, application, or service characteristics. Five phrases that need a follow-up Marketing phrase What it may communicate What to ask next “Low VOC” VOC content lower than some reference Numeric value, basis, category, region, and layer “Zero VOC” Value below a stated threshold or definition Definition, test basis, tint/additives, and full-system values “100% solids” Manufacturer’s formulation/solids description SDS hazards, mixed-product handling, cure, and actual emissions data “Water-based” Water is part of the carrier system Other ingredients, SDS controls, ventilation, and cure conditions “Low odour” Sensory claim under unspecified conditions Product-specific evidence, site controls, and re-entry criteria None of these phrases proves a product is harmless. None establishes wear resistance or adhesion either. Use the SDS for hazards, not for sales comparison alone CCOHS explains that SDSs contain sixteen sections addressing identification, hazards, composition, first aid, firefighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls and PPE, physical properties, stability, toxicology, and other information ( CCOHS SDS guide ). For a two-component coating, obtain the SDS for each component and understand the mixed-product procedure. Include cleaners, repair products, primers, solvents, and topcoats. Review: hazard classifications and statements; routes of exposure; required ventilation or engineering controls; skin, eye, and respiratory protection; incompatible materials and ignition concerns; spill, first-aid, storage, and disposal instructions; revision date and Canadian supplier information. An SDS is a safety communication document. The product data sheet supplies application limits and performance information; the system specification connects the layers; the site hazard assessment determines controls. VOC content is not an emissions timeline Content describes material composition under a defined calculation. Indoor concentration over time depends on quantity, surface area, application and cure, temperature, air exchange, room volume, air pathways, and other products in use. A low content number does not automatically produce a safe re-entry time for every building. Health Canada recommends source control and ventilation as ways to improve indoor air, including following label directions and increasing ventilation during renovations ( Health Canada VOC guidance ). For occupied work, translate that principle into a site plan: isolate the zone, identify exhaust and replacement-air routes, protect nearby intakes, manage open containers and waste, and define who authorizes access. If a project requires an indoor-emissions certification or chamber-test result, state the exact required standard and product. Do not substitute a VOC-content value. Compare complete systems with a worksheet Create one row for every layer and product used in meaningful quantity. Layer/task Product and region VOC value/basis Key SDS hazards Quantity Controls Occupancy criterion Cleaner Repair Primer Body coat Topcoat This prevents a “zero-VOC topcoat” from representing a system that also uses another primer or cleaner. It also connects the product decision to the amount used and task timing. Questions for homes and occupied facilities Which rooms and HVAC paths connect to the work area? Can occupants relocate, and who may need a more conservative plan? Where will exhaust discharge and replacement air enter? Will winter heating or summer humidity affect ventilation and cure? What happens to mixed leftovers, wipes, containers, and solvent? Which product-specific criteria govern worker entry, other trades, and normal occupancy? Who receives an odour or symptom report, and who can pause work? Do not promise that a product will cause no symptoms. If someone has health concerns or experiences effects, move them away from exposure and seek appropriate medical or poison-control advice using the exact product information. The decision rule Use VOC data to compare like products under the same definition and to check applicable regulatory requirements. Use SDSs and a hazard assessment to manage health and safety. Use product data and system evidence to judge application and service. Use a ventilation and access plan to protect occupied spaces. Keeping those four decisions separate makes the VOC number more useful, not less. It becomes one documented input instead of a vague promise about the whole floor. This article is general education, not an exposure assessment or medical, regulatory, or ventilation determination. Use current Canadian documents and qualified site-specific advice. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Health Canada: Volatile organic compounds Health Canada · Official explanation of VOC sources, possible health effects, and exposure reduction. ECCC: VOC Concentration Limits for Architectural Coatings Regulations Environment and Climate Change Canada · Official overview of federal VOC concentration limits for architectural coating categories. CCOHS: Safety Data Sheets Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Canadian guidance on SDS content and use.
