## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/kitchen-bathroom-epoxy-floors/
Kitchen and Bathroom Epoxy Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Can you put an epoxy floor in a kitchen or bathroom? Yes, on concrete. Epoxy bonds to prepared concrete, so kitchens and bathrooms on a slab are good candidates: basement suites, walkout levels, and homes with concrete floors on the main level. Kitchens and bathrooms are among the spaces Final Finish coats. The questions are about what is under the current floor, how the room handles water, and how the work fits around a household. It starts with what is under the floor A concrete slab. The usual candidate. It is ground and prepared like any other floor. Tile on concrete. The tile and its thinset come up first, down to sound concrete. That is demolition, and it should be scoped as its own step. Sheet vinyl or plank on concrete. It comes up, and the adhesive left behind is ground off. A wood subfloor. A wood-framed floor flexes in ways concrete does not, and concrete coating systems are not made for it. That is a different conversation, so raise it early. Water, grip, and the bathroom Bathrooms get wet, and so do the people in them. A smooth, glossy floor can be slippery with water on it. An anti-slip top coat adds grip without looking like a rubber mat. The CCOHS guidance on preventing slips, trips, and falls points to the walking surface as a key factor, and a wet bathroom floor is the textbook case. Our slip resistance guide goes further. Around tubs, showers, and toilets, the coating has to stop cleanly, or run under fixtures that come out for the install. Water should never be able to get under an edge. Ask how each edge will be finished. Cabinets, fixtures, and other trades Kitchens and bathrooms are full of things fastened to the floor. Decide early: Do the cabinets and island come out, or does the floor stop at the toe kick? Does the toilet come out? That usually means a plumber to remove and reset it. What about the appliances, the vanity, and the dishwasher? Coating under removed fixtures gives the cleanest result. Stopping at the cabinets is quicker, but it leaves an edge. Either works if it is decided before the quote. Odour and living in the house Coating materials have an odour while they go down and while they cure, and kitchens and bathrooms are inside the living space. Ventilation, the product choice, and where the household stays during the install all matter. Health Canada’s guidance on indoor air quality is plain about it: when renovating, open the windows and ventilate. The odours and ventilation guide covers what to ask before the work starts. Choosing a finish for the room Kitchen. A metallic floor makes a statement in an open kitchen. A solid colour looks clean and modern. Flake hides crumbs and wear in a busy family kitchen. Bathroom. Flake or solid with an anti-slip top coat for everyday bathrooms, metallic where the look matters more. Mudroom and laundry. Flake with grip. See mudroom floor coatings . Try them on your own room with the floor visualizer , or browse the finish library . The finish comparison sets out the trade-offs. Basement suites and rentals Basement suites are one of the best cases for a coated floor. The slab is already there, the floor is quick to clean between tenants, and there is no carpet or underlay to replace or to hold spills. Check the slab for moisture first, because a coating sits on top of whatever the concrete is doing. The basement guide covers moisture and preparation. Schedule the work between tenancies if you can. An empty suite is faster to clear, easier to ventilate, and nobody has to live around the install. Where the coating meets other floors In most homes the coated kitchen or bathroom meets another floor at a doorway: hardwood, carpet, or tile. Plan those transitions before the quote. A transition strip covers the joint, and the heights on each side should be close enough that nobody trips. Coating to a clean, straight edge under a door is neater than stopping at a ragged line. Comfort and cleaning A coated floor is as hard underfoot as the concrete under it. Rugs by the sink and the tub help, and in-floor heat makes any hard floor comfortable. Cleaning is simple: a soft broom or dust mop, then a damp mop with a mild cleaner. Skip harsh abrasives. The cleaning guide has the details. Planning the job Send photos of the room, the current flooring, and the fixtures through the quote form , and say which fixtures you would like removed. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit. More on residential epoxy flooring and basement floor coatings . Questions people ask Can an epoxy floor go over tile? Not as a finished floor. The tile and its adhesive come up, down to sound concrete, which is then ground and coated. Coating over tile would copy every grout line and rely on a bond to the tile's glaze. Is an epoxy bathroom floor slippery? A smooth, glossy coating can be slippery when wet. An anti-slip top coat adds grip, and it is a sensible choice for a bathroom. Can epoxy go on a wood subfloor? Floor coating systems for concrete are made for concrete, not for wood floors that flex. A wood subfloor needs a different approach, so raise it at the start. Do cabinets have to come out for an epoxy kitchen floor? Not always. The coating can stop at the cabinets, or the cabinets can come out so it runs underneath. Decide before the quote, because it changes both the scope and the finished look. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading CCOHS: Prevention of slips, trips and falls Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety · Walking surfaces, housekeeping, and footwear in slip and fall prevention. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Ventilation during renovations and when using chemical products. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/levelling-concrete-before-coating/
Levelling a Floor Before Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Why levelling comes before coating A floor coating is thin. It follows the concrete under it, so a dip, a lip, or a ridge in the slab shows through the finished floor. Levelling deals with those first: grinding down what is high, filling what is low, and smoothing the transitions. Final Finish does concrete levelling and restoration as part of its concrete work, alongside repair and diamond grinding. Flat is not the same as level Two words, two different things: Flat means the surface has no bumps or dips over a short distance. A flat floor can still slope. Level means the floor is horizontal overall. Garages are usually not meant to be level. They slope toward the overhead door or a floor drain so meltwater runs out instead of pooling. Levelling a garage does not mean taking that slope away. It means taking out the low spots where water sits, the lips at cracks, and the ridges at old patches, so the floor drains the way it was built to. Large commercial floors put numbers on this. ASTM E1155 defines the FF and FL numbers used to measure flatness and levelness. Most homes do not need that precision, but the idea is the same: measure, then correct. Finding the problems A long straightedge , laid across the floor in different directions, shows dips and humps. Light under the edge means a low spot. Water tells the truth in a garage. After washing the floor, watch where the puddles stay. A laser level maps a larger floor quickly. Note the lips at cracks, where one side has lifted, and the edges of old patches. Those catch tires and show through a coating as ridges. Grinding the high spots Diamond grinding brings down high spots, lips, and ridges. The same grinding that prepares the surface for the coating can take a little more off where the floor stands proud. It is precise, and it is also finite: grinding removes millimetres, not centimetres. The diamond grinding guide explains the equipment and the edge work. Filling the low spots Low spots, pits, and spalls are filled with repair materials made for the job. The material has to suit the depth, the traffic, and the coating that goes over it. The ICRI guide to selecting repair materials is the reference for matching a material to a repair. For larger areas, a self-levelling underlayment or topping can bring a section back to plane. It has to be compatible with the coating system and allowed to cure before coating. Our repair mortars guide covers the options. The door strip, the step, and other transitions Transitions are where most levelling work happens in a house: The overhead door strip. The concrete under the door often has a lip, a dip where water sits, or a broken edge from years of freeze-thaw. It is ground, filled, and finished so the door seals and water runs out. The step into the house. The edge of the step chips and the floor at its base collects water. Both are repaired before coating. Where a basement floor meets another floor. A coated slab next to carpet or hardwood needs a transition strip, and the heights should be planned before the coating goes down. Old tile, glue, and patches Basements and older garages often carry the history of past floors. Tile adhesive leaves ridges, old patches leave edges, and some past repairs were never feathered into the slab. Grinding removes adhesive and brings patch edges down flush. Where a patch is loose or hollow, it comes out and is redone with a compatible material, because a coating over a failing patch fails with it. Test the drainage before coating After grinding and filling, a garage floor should be tested the simple way: wet it and watch where the water goes. Any spot that still holds water is easier to fix now than after the coating is down. On a floor with a drain, the water should run to the drain; on one without, it should run out the door. When levelling is not the answer Some unevenness is a symptom. A slab that has settled, heaved, or cracked through may still be moving, and a patch or a coating will not stop that. The ACI guide to floor and slab construction explains how slabs shrink and curl. If a crack is widening, a section rocks underfoot, or the floor has dropped along a wall, the cause needs looking at first. Sometimes the honest answer is that a coating is not the answer yet. The cracks and spalling guide helps sort cosmetic damage from structural questions. What to expect in a quote Levelling work should be named in the quote: where the floor will be ground down, where it will be filled and with what, and whether the slope to the door or drain is kept. Send photos of the dips and lips, ideally with a straightedge or level lying on the floor, through the quote form . Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit. More on the service: concrete solutions . Questions people ask Should a garage floor be level? Usually not. Garage floors are built to slope toward the door or a drain so meltwater runs off. Levelling a garage means removing dips, lips, and ridges while keeping that slope. Can a floor coating hide an uneven floor? No. A coating is thin and follows the concrete under it, so dips, lips, and ridges show through. They are ground down or filled before the coating goes on. What is the difference between a flat floor and a level floor? A flat floor has no bumps or dips over a short distance. A level floor is horizontal overall. A floor can be flat and still sloped, which is exactly what most garages are. Can every uneven floor be fixed before coating? Not always. Settlement, heave, or cracks that are still moving point to a problem below the surface. The cause needs looking at before any levelling or coating. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ASTM E1155-20: Floor Flatness and Levelness Numbers ASTM International · Test method for FF flatness and FL levelness numbers. ICRI Guideline 320.2R-2018 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying materials for the repair of concrete surfaces. ACI PRC-302.1-15: Guide to Concrete Floor and Slab Construction American Concrete Institute · Floor and slab construction, shrinkage, cracking, and curling. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/metallic-epoxy-expectations/
Metallic Epoxy Expectations Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Expect a composition, not a photocopy Metallic epoxy floors are valued for movement, depth, and variation created during placement. Those qualities also mean a small sample or inspiration photo cannot be reproduced line for line across a room. Approve the palette, contrast, overall character, and acceptable variation—not the precise location of every vein or highlight. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Ask the installer to explain which aspects are controlled and which emerge from field application. Colour selection, product ratios, base colour, tools, and broad technique may be controlled. Pigment flow, overlap, temperature, working time, floor geometry, and lighting contribute to individual variation. Build a useful design brief Replace adjectives such as “luxury” or “dramatic” with observable choices: dominant and secondary colours; low, medium, or strong contrast; calmer or more active movement; areas where a visual transition is acceptable; preferred sheen and texture; elements the floor should coordinate with; examples of effects you do not want. View physical samples flat, under the room’s actual lighting. Edmonton’s long winter evenings make artificial light especially relevant. Look from doorways and seated height, not only directly above. Glossy finishes can reflect windows, fixtures, and surface shape strongly; test the room rather than judging a studio photograph. Ask what the sample approves A labelled mock-up should identify primer or base, metallic product and colours, application method, and clear finish. Confirm whether it is meant to approve colour, texture, sheen, movement, or the whole package. A larger sample can communicate scale better but still cannot predict an exact room-sized pattern. Keep the approved sample, photographs under neutral lighting, and exact product codes. Digital renderings are communication tools, not colour standards. Screens and cameras shift colour and contrast. The slab remains visible in subtle ways A metallic effect may draw attention away from minor variation, but it does not level a slab, correct drainage, stop cracks, or strengthen unsound concrete. Directional reflections can make waves, patch edges, joints, and repairs more noticeable. The ACI concrete-repair guide links evaluation, repair, preparation, material selection, and quality control. Before design approval, map cracks, joints, previous patches, low areas, penetrations, and transitions. Ask which will remain visible and which create planned application boundaries. Moisture questions also stay independent of appearance. ASTM F2170 defines one in-situ relative-humidity method; whether it is used and what result the metallic system accepts must be stated in product documentation and the project scope. Plan the whole-room application Metallic placement benefits from a clear sequence and enough uninterrupted access. Discuss room geometry, columns, doorways, stairs, fixed objects, batch boundaries, crew roles, and the route out of the space. Ask where a stop can occur without creating an unintended visual line. Dust, insects, water, and unplanned foot traffic can interrupt a decorative surface. Define barriers, ventilation, lighting, and who can enter while each layer develops. The current product documents should govern mixing, working time, environmental conditions, recoat, and return to use. Balance sheen, traction, and maintenance The protective finish affects reflection, walking feel, and cleaning. No decorative name guarantees traction. Discuss wet use, footwear, slope, cleaning products, and any need for traction media. More texture may change both the look and cleaning effort. Ask for a maintenance guide covering approved cleaners, tools, spill response, mats, furniture feet, and recoating. Use the slip-resistance planning guide to describe real conditions rather than request a vague “non-slip metallic floor.” Repairs may remain visible Metallic patterns are especially difficult to patch invisibly because the original flow cannot be recreated exactly and the surrounding surface changes with use. Before buying, ask how a localized scratch, chip, or substrate repair would be approached. A joint, doorway, or whole section may provide a more honest boundary than a tiny spot. Retain leftover colour identifiers and the installed-system record, not unlabelled mixed product. A future professional needs to know every layer and its recoat preparation. Use three viewing moments at handover Inspect the finished appearance after the manufacturer permits access, then again after temporary barriers and work lighting are removed. View it in daylight, normal evening light, and the primary direction of travel. Record agreed punch-list observations before furniture returns. Judge the floor against the approved design brief, not a single social-media photograph. Natural variation that fits the agreed palette and movement is different from debris, an unintended stop line, missed edge, or coating defect. Ask the contractor to explain which observation is decorative variation and which requires correction under the written scope. Furnishing can change the composition Large rugs, counters, display cases, and seating divide the visible pattern. Put a scaled furniture plan beside the floor plan before choosing a focal area. Confirm when rugs and pads may be placed and whether their backing is compatible. Furniture feet and moving methods should follow the coating and furniture suppliers’ instructions. If a future tenant may remove those objects, remember that covered and exposed areas can age differently. That possibility is another reason to keep the complete system and colour record rather than relying on a project photograph. The written approval should name the complete system, palette, mock-up, acceptable variation, sheen or texture, planned transitions, preparation, repair assumptions, and maintenance. Denis must verify whether Final Finish Epoxy offers metallic systems and confirm all samples, products, scheduling, and performance statements. This guide sets realistic design expectations; it promises no exact pattern or project result. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/mudroom-floor-coating/
Edmonton Mudroom Floor Coatings | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A small room can carry a large workload A mudroom compresses wet boots, pet traffic, grit, bags, benches, mats, and frequent cleaning into a few square metres. Planning should follow the path from exterior door to the rest of the home. Mark where snow drops, where footwear comes off, where water pools, and where people pivot while carrying groceries or children. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . The coating decision comes after that map. A finish cannot correct a leaking threshold, missing weather seal, poor exterior grading, or standing water. Resolve building and drainage problems with the appropriate trade before treating the floor as the solution. Inspect every transition Mudrooms contain edges: exterior threshold, interior doorway, stairs, baseboard, cabinets, drains, and perhaps tile or wood. Measure door clearances and note height changes. Ask how preparation reaches beneath trim and along walls, where the coating ends, and whether a cove or vertical return is included. Look for cracks, soft patches, old adhesive, paint, efflorescence, and dark edges. If the room is below grade or has a water history, document it. The ACI concrete-repair guide treats condition assessment, repair, preparation, and protective-system selection as connected work; that is the right order here too. Design the wet-day routine Walk through a February arrival. Which door opens? Where is the first dry step? Can a mat lie flat without blocking the door? Where does meltwater go? Can the mat be lifted easily for cleaning? Does the family need a clear route while another person removes boots? Mats can capture soil but may trap moisture or interact with a finish. Ask both mat and coating manufacturers about backing compatibility and when a mat can be placed after cure. Do not assume a rubber-backed product is neutral to every topcoat. The Alberta Infrastructure de-icing concrete bulletin discusses de-icers, saturation, freeze-thaw exposure, and spring washing. A home mudroom differs from infrastructure, yet the bulletin reinforces sensible housekeeping: remove tracked de-icing residue rather than allowing it to accumulate. Follow the installed finish’s maintenance instructions. Choose appearance with soil in mind View colour samples on the floor under morning and evening light. Medium contrast or flake may make routine grit less visually dominant, while a solid light or dark colour may reveal certain soils sooner. Neither is inherently more practical. Place representative boot grit and pet hair on a sample to judge visibility. At a stair or level change, deliberate contrast may be more useful than visual continuity. Discuss edges separately from the field. The flake and colour design guide offers a repeatable sample test. Texture is a trade-off, not a checkbox Wet footwear and melted snow make traction important, but “non-slip” is not a responsible promise. Footwear, contamination, slope, cleaning, wear, and surface texture interact. A more textured finish can require more agitation to clean; a smoother one may feel different when wet. Describe the actual users, including children, pets, older adults, or mobility aids, and ask how the proposed texture was selected. Decide where water containment and prompt cleaning support the surface choice. Our slip-resistance guide helps make these conditions explicit. Plan cleaning before selecting the topcoat List household cleaners, disinfectants, pet products, and ice-melt residue likely to reach the floor. Request written compatibility and a care method for the exact topcoat. Confirm acceptable brushes, pads, mop systems, and spill response. Never mix cleaners or improvise with solvent. Storage can undermine cleaning. Allow access beneath shoe racks and benches or make fixed bases part of the edge detail. Protect cabinet ends and adjacent finishes during washing, and decide where dirty water is collected. Keep the entrance working during installation If this is the main household entrance, create an alternate route before work. Include pets, deliveries, emergencies, and access to utilities in the plan. Clarify who moves appliances or built-ins and where belongings are stored away from dust. Ask for separate restrictions for foot traffic, replacing benches, putting down mats, wet cleaning, and full use. The product document and recorded conditions should govern rather than a generic “next day” assumption. Plan for the first week, not just installation day Set aside clean indoor footwear and an alternate entrance through every restricted stage. Keep delivery instructions visible and tell household members when pets may use the route. Do not protect an early-stage floor with cardboard, plastic, or a mat unless the installer confirms that covering is permitted. When the room reopens, introduce benches, hooks, trays, and mats in the agreed sequence. Lift each item after initial use to check for trapped moisture, marking, or unstable feet. If a cabinet or bench rocks, correct the furniture rather than allowing a point to scrape repeatedly. Create a seasonal check at the first major thaw: inspect threshold seals, mat edges, corners, joints, and the main wet path; clean by the approved method; and photograph any change. This links the finish to the building maintenance it depends on. Leave the maintenance card where future residents or cleaners can find it, and transfer the system record if ownership changes. A useful proposal states preparation, crack and edge treatment, complete layer sequence, colour and texture, threshold details, containment, ventilation, cleanup, maintenance, and return-to-use stages. Denis must verify Final Finish Epoxy’s products, service scope, schedule, and warranty before publication. This guide does not promise traction, waterproofing, or correction of drainage and building-envelope defects. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading Alberta Infrastructure: De-Icing Concrete Government of Alberta · Technical bulletin on de-icers, concrete durability, and spring washing. ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · Concrete repair and protective-system selection guidance. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/new-concrete-before-floor-coating/
New Concrete Before Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 22, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor How long should new concrete wait before it is coated? Long enough to cure, and to dry to the coating’s limit. New concrete gains strength over weeks, and it holds a lot of water while it does. Coating manufacturers set a minimum age and a moisture limit for their products, and a moisture test confirms the slab has reached it. On a new-build garage, that often means the coating goes down well after move-in. It is worth the wait. A coating applied over a slab that is still wet can trap that moisture, then blister or lose its bond. Curing and drying are not the same thing Curing is the chemical reaction that hardens concrete. It needs water and time, and it carries on for weeks after the pour. The ACI guide to curing covers how curing is done and why it matters for strength and surface quality. Drying is the slab giving up the extra water that was needed to place and finish it. A slab can be well cured and still too wet for a coating. That is why a moisture test is the real gate, not the calendar. ASTM F2170 describes measuring relative humidity inside the slab, and the product documents say what reading is acceptable. Our moisture testing guide explains the options. What the builder may have put on the surface New slabs often get a curing compound or a sealer sprayed on after finishing. It helps the concrete cure. It also stops a coating from bonding, so it has to come off, and it is not always visible. Ask your builder what was applied, and keep the answer for your coating contractor. New floors can also carry a weak, powdery top layer called laitance, left when water and fine material rise to the surface during finishing. It can look smooth and solid, but a coating bonded to it is only as strong as that thin layer. Grinding removes it. The ICRI guideline on surface preparation explains why the prepared surface has to suit the coating system, and new concrete is no exception. The finish on the slab matters too Garage slabs are often trowelled to a smooth, dense finish. That surface is easy to sweep and hard for a coating to grip until it is ground open. A broom finish is rougher, but it can still carry laitance. Either way, the preparation is diamond grinding, and the surface profile guide explains what an open surface means in practice. The diamond grinding guide covers the equipment. Cracks and joints in a new slab New concrete shrinks as it dries. That is why slabs have control joints, cuts that give the shrinkage a place to crack neatly. Hairline cracks in the first months are common and usually cosmetic. The ACI guide to floor and slab construction explains shrinkage, curling, and joint spacing. For a coating, the useful questions are simple. Are the cracks stable, or still moving? Where are the joints, and will the coating bridge them or stop at them? Cosmetic crack filling is part of the preparation. A crack that keeps growing is a question for the builder first. Why the wait pays off Waiting feels like lost time when the garage is right there. The alternative costs more. A coating over wet concrete can blister as moisture pushes up under it, or let go in patches where it never bonded properly. Fixing that means grinding the failed coating off and starting again, on a floor that now has to be prepared twice. A few extra weeks before the first coat is the cheaper path. Living with the slab before it is coated If you move in before the floor is coated, a few habits keep the concrete ready for it: Catch drips. Oil and fluids soak into new concrete fast. A drip tray under each vehicle saves grinding later. The oil stain guide explains why soaked-in oil is hard to remove. Rinse out the salt. In the first winter, sweep and rinse meltwater and road salt out of the garage rather than letting it dry on the floor. Skip the sealer. If you plan to coat, ask the builder not to add a sealer or hardener on top, or at least to tell you exactly what went on. Avoid rubber mats and tape. Some leave residue or stains that have to be ground away. A new-build checklist Before booking a coating on new concrete, gather: The pour date. What curing compound, sealer, or hardener was applied, if any. Whether the slab has in-floor heat. See coating a heated garage floor . Any cracks, and whether they have changed. Whether a moisture test has been done, when, and the result. Plan early, book later You can choose a finish, get an estimate, and plan the timing long before the slab is ready. Final Finish gives free estimates from photos or an in-person visit, so a new-build garage can be quoted as soon as it is clear. Send photos and the pour date through the quote form , and read about garage floor coating in Edmonton . Questions people ask How long do I have to wait to coat a new concrete floor? Until the slab meets the coating's minimum age and moisture limit. The product's documents set both, and a moisture test confirms the slab is ready. The calendar alone is not the test, because drying depends on the slab, the weather, and the space. Is the white film on my new garage floor a problem? It may be a curing compound, a sealer, or efflorescence. Curing compounds and sealers stop a coating from bonding and have to be removed by grinding. Ask your builder what was applied and pass the answer on to your contractor. Are cracks in a new garage floor normal? Hairline shrinkage cracks are common as new concrete dries, which is why slabs have control joints. Cosmetic cracks are filled before coating. A crack that keeps widening is a question for the builder first. Can I get an estimate before the new concrete is ready? Yes. You can choose a finish and get an estimate from photos early, then book the install once the slab has cured and tested dry enough for the product. Residential epoxy flooring Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-308-16: Guide to External Curing of Concrete American Concrete Institute · Curing practices, materials, and monitoring. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Standard test for relative humidity inside a concrete slab. ICRI Guideline 310.2R-2013 International Concrete Repair Institute · Selecting and specifying concrete surface preparation for sealers, coatings, and overlays. ACI PRC-302.1-15: Guide to Concrete Floor and Slab Construction American Concrete Institute · Floor and slab construction, shrinkage, cracking, and curling. Keep exploring Related floor guides Concrete Moisture Testing Guide ↗ Concrete Surface Profile (CSP) ↗ Diamond Grinding for Floor Prep ↗

## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/office-floor-coating-planning/
Plan an Office Floor Coating Job | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Start with a day in the office Before discussing products, map how the workplace functions from opening to close. Mark entrances, exits, reception, washrooms, lunch areas, meeting rooms, server or electrical rooms, delivery paths, accessible routes, and spaces that cannot close together. Note after-hours occupants such as cleaners, security, and maintenance staff. For local scope options, see our commercial epoxy flooring . Then identify what flooring work changes: noise during preparation, dust risk, odour or vapour controls, furniture relocation, blocked paths, power needs, and cure protection. A promise of “low disruption” has no meaning until these constraints are written. Assign decisions before the work Name one facility contact and one contractor contact for every shift. Define who can release an area, authorize building-system changes, approve newly found repairs, communicate with occupants, and reopen the space. Include property management and the landlord where leases divide those responsibilities. The plan should align with the employer’s occupational-health and emergency procedures. Flooring contractors can provide product and task information, but they should not invent the office’s evacuation, accommodation, security, or ventilation policy. Phase by functional zone Phasing is more useful than simply dividing square footage. A phase must have a safe route around it, a place for furniture, access for equipment, a defined stopping edge, and enough time for every layer and restriction. For each phase, record: last time occupants may enter; furniture, records, and IT equipment to move; preparation and application window; barrier and sign locations; available exits, washrooms, and accessible routes; ventilation and security arrangements; inspection, cleaning, and reopening authority; contingency if conditions delay cure. The commercial downtime planning guide helps turn these fields into an operational schedule. Control dust before discussing odour Mechanical preparation can affect nearby work through noise and dust. Ask for the equipment, collection method, edge-work approach, barrier plan, waste route, and cleanup acceptance. Protect sensitive electronics and records according to facility requirements; do not assume a closed office door provides adequate containment. Trace building airflow with facilities personnel. Identify supply and return grilles, shared air handlers, stairwells, lifts, and door pressure. Only authorized personnel should alter HVAC operation. Treat air claims carefully Health Canada identifies paints, varnishes, glues, and other products as possible sources of volatile organic compounds and advises following label directions and using proper ventilation. Request current safety and technical data sheets for every repair material, primer, coating, cleaner, and solvent. Have the workplace’s qualified reviewer determine controls. “Low odour” does not establish low risk, and a smell check does not establish readiness. Health Canada’s indoor-air guidance recommends increased ventilation during renovation work; the facility team must decide how that general advice applies to the actual building and outdoor conditions. Inventory objects before they become change orders List desks, partitions, millwork, rolling files, safes, appliances, floor outlets, cables, door stops, baseboards, and equipment fixed to the slab. Identify who disconnects, moves, stores, protects, and reinstalls each item. Photograph walls and furniture before movement. Confirm whether the finish extends beneath movable items, fixed cabinetry, and modular partitions. Define treatment at carpet, tile, lifts, thresholds, and base. A clean transition detail often matters more to daily use than the centre of the room. Reopening needs multiple criteria Do not base reopening solely on a surface feeling dry. Product documents may distinguish foot traffic, furniture, rolling loads, cleaning, and chemical exposure. Add facility criteria: barriers removed, routes restored, housekeeping completed, ventilation returned to approved operation, signs removed, alarms or security checked, and punch-list items isolated. The person who opens the office should have a short signed checklist, not a verbal message. Keep maintenance instructions and the installed-system record available to cleaners and facilities staff. Make the proposal operational A useful office proposal names preparation, repairs, system layers, site-condition limits, noise and dust controls, air-information responsibilities, phases, furniture scope, transitions, cleaning, waste, return-to-use stages, and change process. Unknown substrate conditions should be identified rather than hidden. Communicate by audience Occupants need simple information: affected area, dates, alternate routes, expected noise, who to contact, and what not to move. Security needs authorized names, access hours, keys, alarms, and delivery rules. Cleaners need barriers, approved products, and reopening status. Building operations needs power, ventilation, loading, waste, and emergency details. Prepare each notice from the same phase plan so instructions do not conflict. Update the revision date when timing changes and remove obsolete signs. A message saying “floor work this weekend” is not enough for someone arriving to find an accessible route closed. Close each phase before starting another Use a turnover walk to record edges, transitions, colour, texture, cleanliness, access restoration, and outstanding items. Photograph the completed area before furniture returns. If a defect or delay affects the next phase, revise the sequence instead of allowing the same issue to propagate. Hold a brief post-project review with facilities and cleaning staff. Capture what affected occupants, which controls worked, and which maintenance questions remain. That record improves later recoats or additional floors in the building. Archive phase maps, product records, notices, and maintenance instructions together so facilities teams do not reconstruct the job from invoices alone. Use the contractor question guide to verify documentation and responsibility. Denis must confirm Final Finish Epoxy’s actual commercial services, products, safety practices, schedule, credentials, and warranty before publication. Site management and qualified facility professionals retain responsibility for workplace-specific controls and occupancy decisions. Health Canada: Improve indoor air quality in your home Health Canada · Includes renovation and chemical-product ventilation guidance. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/polyaspartic-flooring-neutral-guide/
Polyaspartic Floors Neutral Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor The chemistry name is only the first line Polyaspartic products are often discussed as if the category were a complete floor specification. It is not. A buyer still needs the exact product, substrate assessment, preparation, repair plan, layer sequence, application conditions, decorative finish, maintenance instructions, and return-to-use stages. For local scope options, see our epoxy flooring services . Use neutral language when comparing options. Claims such as “better than epoxy,” “one-day,” or “UV proof” compress many variables into a slogan. Ask which current technical document supports the claim for the named product and the proposed use. Read the proposal from concrete upward Have the contractor list every layer: repairs, primer if used, base or body coat, flake or aggregate, and topcoat. Polyaspartic material may be used in one or several positions; do not assume the same chemistry throughout. For each layer, record manufacturer, product, intended function, application amount or thickness, recoat requirements, and compatibility with the layers around it. If manufacturers are mixed, ask who accepted that interface in writing. The hybrid flooring guide provides a system-stack worksheet. Concrete condition still sets the starting point Fast application does not shorten assessment. Look for weak concrete, contamination, old coatings, cracks, joints, repairs, drainage, and moisture indicators. Ask how the surface will be cleaned and mechanically prepared, what profile the product requires, and how edges and drains are treated. The ACI concrete-repair guide connects evaluation, surface preparation, repair, material selection, and quality control. That sequence is useful regardless of coating chemistry. If moisture evaluation is relevant, specify the test and product limit. ASTM F2170 defines an in-situ relative-humidity method for concrete slabs; it does not set one acceptable result for every polyaspartic product or layer. Ask whether the proposed test, slab condition, and result meet the complete manufacturer’s system requirements. A faster reaction changes planning Some products in this category may have relatively short working and recoat periods under stated conditions. That can be useful for scheduling, but it demands crew, batch, tool, and transition planning. Ask how application time changes with material, slab, and ambient temperature and how the crew prevents seams or missed edges. The proposal should state who records mixing and application times, temperature, humidity, and any other conditions required by the data sheet. It should also explain what happens if a recoat window is missed. Mechanical preparation or another documented step may be required; the answer must come from the current product instructions. A quick foot-traffic milestone does not automatically authorize furniture, mats, vehicles, cleaning, or chemical exposure. Request each stage separately and establish what event starts the clock. Appearance comes from more than resin In a flake floor, base colour, chip blend, broadcast density, clear-film build, sheen, and traction media shape the result. Approve a labelled physical sample and record exact codes. Ask whether flakes are lightly scattered or fully broadcast and how the intended texture is created. For exposed sunlight near overhead doors or windows, ask for product-specific colour and gloss information rather than category claims. A topcoat’s documented weathering or light-exposure properties do not automatically describe materials beneath it or guarantee no change. Compare real exposures List what the floor will meet: hot tires, tracked de-icing residue, grit, welding, rolling loads, cleaners, oils, sunlight, or wet footwear. Then ask which manufacturer test data and limitations are relevant. Do not translate one laboratory result into a universal lifespan or warranty. Traction is also system- and condition-specific. Texture, contaminants, footwear, slope, cleaning, and wear interact. Ask how a selected traction additive affects appearance and cleaning rather than accepting “non-slip” as a product feature. Maintenance and repair should be decided now Request approved cleaners, tools, spill response, mat restrictions, inspection points, and recoat preparation. Ask how a scratch, chip, or localized delamination is repaired and where a visually honest boundary can fall. Decorative flake and aged sheen may make invisible repair unrealistic. Keep the full installed-system record, not only the topcoat name. A future repair professional needs every layer, application date, and maintenance history. Put category claims through a three-part test When a proposal makes a performance statement, ask for three linked items: the named product and test or technical document; the project condition that makes the information relevant; and the limitation or maintenance requirement that accompanies it. If any part is missing, the claim is not ready to guide selection. For example, a published result for one topcoat does not automatically describe the primer, repair layer, decorative broadcast, or concrete bond. A stated application range does not prove that every part of an Edmonton garage slab will remain within it. The contractor’s quality-control plan closes the gap between product information and field conditions. Before signing, compare the polyaspartic proposal against at least one complete alternative using identical rows for preparation, layers, closure, use, maintenance, repair, documentation, and warranty. This keeps the decision about the floor rather than the marketing category. Keep the site photographs and final sample too. Replace unsupported shorthand in the proposal with exact product language, then keep the approved sample, colour record, maintenance guide, comparison, and cited documents in the selection record. This neutral guide does not state that Final Finish Epoxy sells polyaspartic flooring. Denis must verify any offered system, product compatibility, schedule, warranty, credential, or performance statement before publication. A site-specific written scope and current manufacturer documents—not the category name—govern selection. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/polyurea-flooring-neutral-guide/
Polyurea Flooring: Neutral Guide | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Polyurea is a family, not one performance profile The word “polyurea” can appear in descriptions of products with different formulations, application methods, and roles. A product may be one layer within a larger system. Buyers should therefore compare exact technical documents and the installed stack, not make decisions from the chemistry name alone. For local scope options, see our epoxy flooring services . Start by asking: where in the floor is the polyurea product used, and what job is it meant to perform? Request a layer-by-layer answer The proposal should identify repair materials, primer, body coat, decorative media, intermediate coats, and topcoat. Beside every layer, list exact product, manufacturer, required preparation, mixing or equipment, application conditions, stated film build, recoat requirements, and return-to-use restrictions. Ask whether the assembly is a published manufacturer system. If it combines sources, request written compatibility support. A layer that bonds well to prepared concrete still has to accept the next layer, and a topcoat has to bond to the decorative or body layer beneath it. Do not let speed skip diagnosis Fast reaction or return-to-service language can be attractive, especially where an Edmonton garage or business has limited closure time. Yet the concrete still needs inspection, cleaning, preparation, and repair. Shorter product working time can make planning more demanding, not less. The ACI concrete-repair guide treats condition evaluation, surface preparation, repair, selection, and quality control as one process. Ask how cracks, joints, weak areas, oil, old coatings, edges, drains, and previous patches are handled before mixing begins. Moisture claims need boundaries No category-wide statement proves suitability for a damp or moisture-affected slab. Ask what condition was observed, which test is proposed, and what the exact product documents permit. ASTM F2170 establishes an in-situ relative-humidity test method for concrete slabs. The selected manufacturer, not the standard title, provides the acceptance criteria for its system. A moisture-related primer does not automatically resolve hydrostatic pressure, water entry, drainage, or incompatibility in other layers. If a mitigation layer is proposed, ask what it is designed to address and what conditions remain excluded. Installation planning is part of product suitability Some polyurea products require specialized application equipment or have limited working time. Confirm how the contractor manages proportioning or mixing, batch size, material temperature, slab and ambient conditions, edge work, crew coordination, and planned stopping points. The correct answers depend on the named product. Ask which readings and times become part of the project record. A short window between layers needs a contingency: if preparation, weather, access, or equipment interrupts the sequence, what documented step allows work to resume? Return to use should be divided into foot traffic, furniture or equipment, mats, cleaning, vehicles, rolling loads, and chemical service. Do not infer all of these from the earliest milestone on a data sheet. Evaluate the finish occupants actually touch The top layer determines much of the floor’s initial sheen, texture, colour response, and maintenance, regardless of what chemistry appears lower in the stack. Ask about UV or exterior-light exposure, wet conditions, footwear, tires, cleaners, impact, and rolling traffic. Avoid absolute claims such as “will not fade,” “will not scratch,” or “is chemical proof.” Request product-specific data and limitations relevant to actual exposure. Laboratory tests can inform selection but do not establish a project lifespan. Texture requires the same care. More surface relief may change traction and cleaning effort. No product is universally slip-proof because contamination, slope, footwear, cleaning, and wear all contribute. Look ahead to inspection and repair Ask the installer to describe routine cleaning, approved products and tools, mat compatibility, spill response, inspection, and recoat preparation. Also ask what a localized repair entails: how a boundary is found, which layers are removed, how remaining material is prepared, and whether a visual difference should be expected. Keep exact product and colour codes, batch information provided at handover, application dates, photographs, and maintenance records. The generic phrase “polyurea floor” will not give a future contractor enough information. For direct comparison, see the neutral polyaspartic buyer’s guide and the hybrid system worksheet . Compare the complete written systems against the same site needs rather than trying to rank names. Ask the crew-planning questions directly Because some products leave little time for adjustment, ask how many trained people are assigned, who mixes or operates equipment, who handles edges, and who watches the wet line and site readings. Confirm the largest practical batch or pass for the room and where an intentional stop would occur. Ask what spare equipment or interruption plan exists for a blocked hose, power loss, product-temperature issue, or newly exposed repair. This is not a demand for proprietary technique; it is a check that the schedule recognizes the selected product’s constraints. Make handover language precise The system record should not say only “polyurea, grey.” It should identify every installed product, colour or blend, layer order, maintenance guide, restrictions, application dates, and contact route. If the manufacturer uses a more specific category name, retain that terminology rather than simplifying it. If a product is replaced before installation, repeat the layer, condition, recoat, maintenance, and compatibility review; similar category names do not make substitutions equivalent. This resource makes no claim that Final Finish Epoxy offers polyurea flooring. Denis must verify all products, compatibility, service scope, scheduling, warranty, credentials, and performance language before publication. The current manufacturer documents and project-specific substrate evidence govern the final decision. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/primer-in-floor-coating-system/
Primer in a Floor Coating System | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Primer is a role, not an automatic extra A primer is the first liquid layer in some floor-coating systems. Depending on the exact product and specification, it may be intended to wet a prepared surface, support adhesion, reduce outgassing risk, create a uniform base, or address a defined moisture condition. Other published systems may not call for a separate primer. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . The useful question is not “Does primer always make a floor better?” It is “Why does this system require this primer on this slab?” Begin with the manufacturer’s system Request the current technical data sheets for primer and next layer. Confirm that they form a documented system and record required surface preparation, mixing, environmental limits, application amount or thickness, recoat conditions, and broadcast instructions if aggregate is used. If products come from different manufacturers, ask who accepted their compatibility in writing. A successful bond between primer and concrete is only half the interface; the next coat must also bond to the primer. The slab comes before the primer Primer does not replace cleaning or mechanical preparation. Oil, sealer, adhesive, curing compounds, laitance, weak concrete, dust, and old coating need condition-specific treatment. Ask how the crew will confirm the required surface profile and cleanliness at edges, corners, drains, cracks, and large open areas. The ACI concrete-repair guide places evaluation, repair, surface preparation, material selection, and quality control in one chain. This prevents primer from being treated as a cure-all for an unknown substrate. Cracks, spalls, joints, and low areas also need separate decisions. Ask whether repairs occur before or after primer, how repair materials are prepared, and which instructions establish compatibility. A primer does not stop structural movement or correct drainage. Ask what problem the layer addresses For a standard adhesion or wetting primer, ask what prepared-surface condition it expects and how pinholes, absorption, or dry areas are checked. For an outgassing-sensitive floor, ask how slab temperature and application timing are controlled and what evidence determines the response. For a moisture-related primer or mitigation layer, request precise boundaries: test method, measured condition, permitted range, required film build, number of coats, quality-control checks, and exclusions. The phrase “moisture barrier” can conceal important differences. ASTM F2170 defines in-situ relative-humidity testing for concrete slabs. It does not decide whether a primer is needed or establish one acceptance limit. The selected product documentation must connect test results to the proposed system. Review the concrete moisture testing guide before accepting a moisture claim. Application quality is visible in records A primer layer can be hidden quickly, so establish a hold point. Record the accepted prepared slab, repair status, product and batch information supplied, mix times, slab and ambient conditions, application start and finish, coverage or thickness checks required by the manufacturer, and the planned next-coat time. Edges and porous or repaired areas may behave differently from the field. Ask how the applicator identifies absorption, pinholes, puddles, missed spots, contamination, or material beyond its working period. The response should follow the product instructions, not an improvised extra coat. Recoat timing protects the interface Primer and body coat must meet within documented conditions. Ask for both minimum and maximum recoat criteria and what preparation is required if the window is exceeded. Keep dust, water, insects, workers, and other trades off the primed surface. Do not assume a tacky feel is the universal signal. Products differ, and field temperature can change timing. The guide to floor-coating recoat windows explains how to record each interface. When a no-primer proposal can be legitimate Some complete systems are designed for direct application to correctly prepared concrete. If a proposal omits primer, ask for the exact manufacturer’s system document and confirm that slab conditions, preparation, application build, and intended use fit. Do not add a primer simply from habit; an unapproved layer can introduce compatibility and scheduling issues. Likewise, do not remove a specified primer merely to save time. Compare proposals by the complete tested or documented system, not by layer count. Five lines the proposal should contain The final scope should identify the primer product and purpose; substrate and repair preparation; acceptance criteria; application and recoat controls; and action for moisture, pinholes, missed windows, or other deviations. Handover records should preserve the full stack for future maintenance. Translate primer into a bid-comparison row When one proposal includes primer and another does not, avoid treating the extra layer as automatic value or automatic waste. Ask both bidders to name the published system, the observed slab condition, and the function performed at the concrete interface. Then compare the complete preparation and layer sequence. Also compare what happens after application. One primer may require a broadcast, another a particular tack or cure state, and a direct-to-concrete body coat may have its own build and timing rules. The number of layers cannot be compared without their functions. At handover, preserve photographs of the accepted primer before it disappears, along with the product name, application time, conditions, and next-coat record promised in the scope. Those details are more useful for future investigation than the phrase “primed floor.” Denis must verify the actual primers, systems, preparation methods, testing, and quality controls used by Final Finish Epoxy before publication. This guide explains specification questions; it does not establish that every project needs primer or that any primer can solve moisture, contamination, cracking, or weak concrete. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/questions-to-ask-floor-coating-contractor/
Ask Your Floor Coating Contractor | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 14, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Ask about the floor before asking about the brand A useful contractor conversation starts with observations. What did they see in the concrete, what remains unknown, and how does that evidence shape preparation and system choice? Product names matter later, when they are tied to a written layer sequence and current technical documents. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . Use the questions below during the site visit. Ask for important answers in the proposal rather than relying on memory. Site condition and measurement Which areas did you inspect, and which were hidden or inaccessible? Stored goods, mats, cabinets, or old flooring can conceal conditions. What cracks, spalls, patches, joints, contamination, old coatings, or moisture indicators did you observe? Request photographs or a marked sketch. How was the project area measured? Confirm floors, steps, curbs, vertical surfaces, and excluded areas. Which building or drainage problems are outside the coating scope? A coating should not be presented as a structural or water-entry repair without evidence. Preparation and repairs How will oil, de-icing residue, old coating, sealer, adhesive, and loose concrete be treated? Cleaning and mechanical profiling solve different problems. Which preparation method and required surface condition apply to the selected system? Ask about edges, drains, posts, steps, and dust collection. How will each crack, joint, and spall be handled? Confirm whether movement can reappear and whether repairs may remain visible. What happens if preparation exposes more damage? The change process should name the decision-maker, documentation, price method, and pause point. The garage preparation guide shows the detail a preparation answer should contain. Moisture and product selection Is moisture investigation warranted here, and why? Ask for test method, locations, timing, results, and the exact product limits. What is every layer in the proposed system? List repair material, primer, body coat, broadcast, intermediate coat, and topcoat by manufacturer and product. Who confirms compatibility? This is especially important when products come from different manufacturers. Which current technical data sheets govern preparation, mixing, site conditions, film build, recoat, and service? Keep copies with the contract. Avoid accepting category claims such as “epoxy lasts longer” or “polyaspartic is always better.” Formulations and complete systems vary. Appearance and real use What exactly does the sample approve? Record base colour, blend, broadcast, texture, sheen, and acceptable variation. How will the floor meet edges, drains, doors, stairs, walls, and adjacent finishes? Transition details prevent later surprises. How did you account for tires, grit, sunlight, water, cleaners, rolling loads, impact, or chemicals? Ask for limitations as well as benefits. How is traction being discussed? No floor is universally slip-proof; contaminant, footwear, slope, texture, wear, and cleaning all matter. Crew, workplace, and site controls Who performs and supervises the work? Ask which tasks may be subcontracted and who is your daily contact. How are dust, noise, ventilation, power, waste, security, and access handled? Include pets and household entry for homes; exits, occupants, and other trades for businesses. Which safety data sheets apply, and who reviews building-specific controls? For workplaces, Alberta provides the official OHS Act, Regulation and Code . The employer and work-site parties must determine applicable duties; a generic proposal is not the site safety plan. How does air move to occupied areas? The Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety explains that indoor air quality concerns can involve sources, ventilation, and occupant information . Qualified site personnel should translate that framework into controls for the actual building. Schedule and return to use What conditions could change the schedule? Slab temperature, ambient conditions, repairs, access, and recoat windows may matter. When can each activity resume? Ask separately about inspection, walking, furniture, mats, cleaning, vehicles, rolling loads, and chemicals. What event starts each waiting period, and where is it documented? A finish feeling dry is not a universal clearance. Who communicates and approves a delay? A realistic contingency is more valuable than an unsupported exact promise. Read how epoxy coatings cure for the reason these milestones should remain separate. Price, handover, and warranty What is included, excluded, allowed for, or unknown? Compare scope before totals. How are taxes, mobilization, storage, furniture moving, repairs, edges, cleanup, and disposal shown? Avoid filling gaps with assumptions. What records are delivered? Request system and colour details, product documents, application or condition records promised in the scope, photographs, and maintenance instructions. What does the warranty actually cover? Separate installer workmanship, manufacturer terms, concrete conditions, exclusions, maintenance, notice, inspection, and remedy. How should a scratch, stain, chip, or localized failure be reported and repaired? Ask about visual limitations. Which company details can I verify? Confirm legal name, contact details, insurance or credentials relevant to the job, and references directly. Use the proposal comparison worksheet to place bidders side by side. A careful contractor may answer some questions with “we need testing” or “we will know after preparation.” That is more useful than false certainty when the unknown and decision process are documented. Denis must verify any Final Finish Epoxy answer about service area, crew, products, methods, schedule, price, warranty, credentials, or performance before publication. This list helps buyers request evidence; it is not a company claim or a substitute for a site-specific contract and safety plan. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/remove-oil-stains-before-floor-coating/
Oil Stains Before Floor Coating | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Oil on a garage floor is more than a dark mark. It can be contamination at the surface, liquid held in pores, or evidence of an active vehicle or equipment leak. A coating decision should begin by finding out which condition you have. Covering the stain before resolving that question can hide useful evidence and makes it harder to write a defensible preparation scope. For local scope options, see our residential epoxy flooring . For an Edmonton garage, start with a simple history. Mark where vehicles normally park, where snow melt collects, which stains are recent, what cleaners were used, and whether the area still feels greasy after drying. Photograph the floor in even light. A few notes now give the assessor more than a freshly washed slab with no context. Stop the source before treating the concrete Fix or contain the leak first. Otherwise, freshly prepared concrete can be contaminated again while the project is being planned. Move leaking equipment to a tray, address the vehicle problem, and keep oily rags or absorbent materials off the slab. If an unknown liquid may be hazardous, follow the product label and local disposal requirements rather than treating it as ordinary wash water. Do not mix cleaners or improvise with solvents. The relevant cleaner, dwell time, agitation, rinsing, recovery, and disposal method depend on the contaminant and the coating manufacturer’s written instructions. A contractor should be able to describe the process without promising that every old stain will disappear visually. Cleaning and mechanical preparation do different jobs Cleaning is intended to remove oil, grease, residue, and cleaning products. Mechanical preparation changes the concrete surface so the specified system can bond to it. One is not a substitute for the other. Grinding or blasting an oily slab can spread contamination, load tooling, or drive residue into adjacent areas; coating over a detergent film creates another problem. The sequence matters. The ACI concrete repair guide is a primary industry reference that covers condition assessment, surface preparation, repair materials, protective systems, and quality control. Its scope supports treating contamination as part of an evaluated concrete-repair process, not as a cosmetic cleaning step. The project specification and current product data sheets still control the actual method. An assessment may divide the floor into zones: sound, apparently clean concrete; visible staining that no longer transfers residue; areas that still release oil after cleaning; cracked, scaled, or previously patched concrete; an old coating with unknown adhesion or contamination beneath it. That map helps prevent a single preparation method from being applied blindly across the whole garage. What can show that the floor is ready? There is no universal household test that proves oily concrete is coatable. Ask what acceptance check the installer and coating manufacturer require. Depending on the written system, that may include visual inspection, checking for residue after cleaning, a small trial area, surface-profile verification, or an adhesion-related check. The important point is to agree on the evidence before the coating arrives, including who decides whether a questionable zone proceeds, receives more preparation, or is excluded. Moisture is a separate question. Darkening caused by oil does not establish the slab’s moisture condition, and a dry-looking surface is not a moisture test. ASTM F2170 describes in-situ relative-humidity testing in concrete floor slabs. When the selected manufacturer requires slab-moisture information, the proposal should name the required test method, timing, locations, and acceptance criteria rather than using oil cleanup as a proxy. If the garage also has scaling, spalls, or cracks around the contaminated area, review the guide to concrete cracks and spalling before coating before comparing repair allowances. Repairs need compatible preparation and cure conditions of their own. Questions that make a quotation clearer Invite the estimator to be specific. Useful questions include: Which areas are considered contaminated, and how will they be isolated from clean concrete? Which cleaner or treatment is proposed, and does its manufacturer permit the intended use? How will spent cleaner, oily water, and debris be contained and disposed of? What mechanical preparation follows cleaning? What result must be observed before primer or coating is applied? What happens if oil returns during preparation? Are deeply affected areas repairable within the quoted scope, or does work pause for a revised decision? Which current product data sheet governs surface condition, moisture, mixing, and application? A useful proposal distinguishes included work from contingencies. “Degrease as required” leaves the most important decision undefined. A better scope identifies the observed zones, planned sequence, acceptance check, and process for concealed conditions. What homeowners can do before the visit Avoid applying sealers, paint, acid, or a new degreaser immediately before the assessment. Keep the floor accessible, but leave enough evidence for the contractor to see the stain pattern. Gather the names of products previously used and, if available, the old coating or patch records. Note whether water beads, darkens the concrete unevenly, or carries an oily sheen after cleaning; report those observations without treating them as pass/fail tests. Edmonton winters add tracked de-icer, sand, water, and road grime to the mix. These are not all “oil,” and they may require different cleaning or repair decisions. The companion guide to winter salt and concrete-floor damage helps separate seasonal deposits from scaling or other concrete deterioration. The practical goal is not a perfectly colourless slab. It is a documented surface condition that the specified coating system permits. Until the contamination, concrete condition, moisture requirements, and acceptance checks are known, the responsible answer is to keep the scope open rather than turn a complex substrate issue into a blanket performance promise. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/resources/repair-or-replace-coated-floor/
Repair or Replace a Coated Floor | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor The choice between repairing and replacing a coated floor is rarely determined by the size of the ugly spot alone. A small blister can point to a broader moisture or adhesion issue; a large worn path may be serviceable if the coating remains bonded and the wear mechanism is understood. The useful question is: what failed, why did it fail, and where does sound material begin? For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . That requires an assessment of both the visible coating and the concrete beneath it. A repair is a system decision, not just colour matching. First, classify what you can see Walk the floor in consistent light and mark each type of concern separately. Do not group every imperfection under “peeling.” Record scratches, loss of gloss, worn texture, impact chips, lifting edges, hollow-sounding zones, blisters, cracks, dampness, white deposits, and failed patches. Photographs should include a wide view and a close view with location notes. Add the age of the observed change if known, recent leaks or flooding, cleaning chemicals, vehicle or cart traffic, and any prior repair. This condition map becomes the basis for a scope that can be compared across proposals. A local repair needs a sound boundary Spot repair is most credible when damage is localized, the cause has stopped, surrounding coating is sound enough to prepare, and the new repair materials are compatible with the existing system. The edge matters: if preparation keeps revealing loose material, the repair boundary may need to expand. The ACI PRC-546 concrete repair guide covers evaluation, repair, surface preparation, protective systems, and quality control. That primary-source framework supports assessing deterioration before selecting a repair material. It does not turn an unknown old coating into a verified compatible base; product identification and current manufacturer instructions remain necessary. Appearance also deserves an honest conversation. Even a technically suitable patch can remain visible because of colour, gloss, texture, aggregate exposure, ageing, or lighting. If a seamless appearance matters, a larger recoat area may be considered even when the functional repair is smaller. That is an aesthetic scope choice, not proof the entire coating has failed. Signs that point toward broader removal Replacement or extensive removal deserves discussion when failure is repeated or widespread, the old coating is poorly bonded across multiple zones, the system is unknown and compatibility cannot be established, contamination extends beyond a local area, or repairs would create a patchwork that does not meet operational needs. Cracking may also change the decision. A coating cannot diagnose structural movement, stop an active leak, or make unstable concrete sound. Significant movement, unexplained displacement, active water entry, or deteriorated concrete should be referred to an appropriately qualified professional before a decorative replacement scope is finalized. If the issue appears limited to scuffs or wear, start with the scratch-maintenance guide for coated floors rather than assuming removal is necessary. If the coating is lifting, the floor-coating site-assessment checklist provides a useful record to bring to the visit. Moisture must be considered separately Surface symptoms can suggest moisture, but they do not establish its source or quantity. Plumbing leaks, exterior drainage, joints, vapour movement, and cleaning practices can produce different patterns. A handheld reading, when used, should not be presented as equivalent to every standardized slab test. ASTM F2170 sets out a method for measuring relative humidity in concrete floor slabs using in-situ probes. If the replacement system’s manufacturer calls for this method, project documents should identify the test edition, locations, conditioning, results, and product-specific acceptance limit. Moisture testing is evidence for a system decision; it is not a generic promise that a repair will succeed. Compare three possible scopes Stabilize and repair Define what is removed, how the boundary is checked, how concrete is repaired, and which layers are reinstated. Include the likely visual difference and the process if loose coating extends farther than expected. Prepare and recoat a larger area This may help unify appearance or renew a worn surface, but only if the retained coating is a permitted substrate. The proposal should state how adhesion, cleanliness, existing texture, and recoat compatibility are evaluated. Remove and replace the system State the removal method, edge and joint treatment, concrete repairs, moisture requirements, new layer sequence, ventilation controls, and staged return to service. “Full replacement” should not conceal exclusions such as inaccessible areas or deeper concrete repair. Questions worth asking before authorizing work Ask the contractor to show the observations behind the recommendation: Where is the coating considered sound, and how was that evaluated? What is the likely failure mechanism, and has its source been addressed? Is the existing product known? Which manufacturer documents support compatibility? How will concealed deterioration change the scope? Which joints and cracks are included, and which require separate review? What visual differences should be expected after a local repair? What are the written environmental, cure, cleaning, and return-to-service restrictions? Avoid choosing solely by the smallest initial area or the broadest recommendation. The strongest planning document connects observed conditions to preparation, materials, checkpoints, and exclusions. Because this resource cannot inspect the floor or verify the existing system, it remains a review-gated guide rather than a claim that any particular Edmonton floor should be repaired or replaced. Keep the photographs, inspection notes, old product records, and accepted scope after the work. If another area changes later, that file makes it easier to compare patterns and determine whether the new concern is local or part of the same mechanism. Concrete preparation Primary references Sources and further reading ACI PRC-546-23: Concrete Repair—Guide American Concrete Institute · A current ACI guide covering concrete repair, protection, preparation, and quality control. ASTM F2170: in-situ relative humidity in concrete slabs ASTM International · Check the current edition and the specified test procedure.
