Winter Salt and Concrete Floors | Final Finish Epoxy

Updated September 18, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor Edmonton winters bring meltwater, grit, and de-icing chemicals onto garage, parkade, loading, and entrance floors. The visible white residue is only part of the story. Water movement, repeated wetting, freezing exposure at edges, existing cracks, and concrete quality all affect what you see. A coating is not a substitute for diagnosing and repairing deteriorated concrete. For local scope options, see our concrete preparation . Read the official Alberta guidance first Alberta Infrastructure’s technical bulletin on de-icing concrete discusses de-icer effects on concrete and calls for thorough spring washing of treated concrete. Use that primary source to frame seasonal care, while following site requirements for containment and discharge. Do not send salty or contaminated wash water to a drain without confirming it is permitted. The bulletin is not a project-specific repair specification. Interior heated slabs, exposed aprons, ramps, and thresholds experience different water and temperature conditions. Make a winter condition map Before deep cleaning, photograph tire paths, door lines, drains, joints, wall edges, ramps, and wet spots. Mark: loose or flaking surface material; shallow scaling or deeper spalls; cracks and displaced edges; rust staining or exposed metal; white deposits and persistent dampness; hollow or failed patches; damage at the warm-to-cold transition; routes where vehicles or footwear deposit slurry. Repeat photographs after cleaning and drying. Appearance alone cannot establish depth or cause, but the pattern helps an assessor distinguish deposits from material loss and choose investigation points. Control water and tracked material Repair leaks and review drainage, door seals, downspouts, grading, and snow-storage practices with appropriate trades. Remove standing water promptly using a method suitable for the facility. Entrance mats and containment can reduce tracking but need cleaning and drying so they do not become saturated reservoirs. Sweep or vacuum grit before wet cleaning to reduce abrasion. Use cleaners and equipment permitted for the concrete or installed coating. Never mix cleaning products. Follow labels and safety data sheets, protect occupants, and manage runoff. Damaged concrete needs a repair decision Soundness, contamination, cracks, reinforcing corrosion, joints, and moisture must be evaluated before coating. The ACI PRC-546 concrete repair guide covers evaluation, concrete removal, preparation, repair materials, protective systems, and quality control. That primary framework supports mapping deterioration and selecting repairs before a protective finish. Deep spalling, exposed or corroded reinforcement, significant displacement, structural concern, or continuing water entry may require an engineer or other qualified professional. Do not fill a moving joint or unstable spall simply to create a flat decorative surface. The concrete cracks and spalling guide helps organize observations for an assessment. Ask how repair edges are cut or prepared, how unsound material is identified, which repair product is compatible, and what cure occurs before coating. Coating selection starts after evaluation Request the complete layer sequence and current manufacturer requirements for substrate, preparation, moisture, temperature, application, cure, chemical exposure, and cleaning. Ask which winter exposures the recommendation is intended to address and which remain owner controls. Avoid blanket claims that a coating is “salt proof” or will stop freeze-thaw damage. The result depends on the exact system, concrete, detailing, exposure, defects, and maintenance. A coating also cannot correct drainage or stop water entering from an unresolved source. At door thresholds and ramps, define terminations deliberately. Snowplows, shovels, tire chains, metal edges, and abrupt transitions may create mechanical damage that needs operational controls or sacrificial details. Plan seasonal maintenance at handover The owner should receive approved cleaning products, dilution, tools, frequency, spill response, inspection points, and prohibited methods. Include a spring inspection after accumulated winter material is removed. Look for chips, worn texture, lifting edges, cracks, dampness, and damaged terminations. Document changes early. A small local repair may be possible when the boundary is sound and compatibility is known; repeated or widespread damage needs a broader diagnosis. Keep the winter log with product and repair records. Bring these questions to the quotation Which observed areas show deposits, scaling, spalling, moisture, or previous repair? What additional assessment is needed before a coating scope? How will de-icer, oil, old coatings, and weak concrete be handled? Which cracks, joints, drains, ramps, and thresholds are included? What inspection proves the substrate is ready for the specified system? What winter cleaning and runoff plan is compatible with the finish? Which damage requires prompt review after installation? Winter salt is a recurring exposure to manage, not a single stain to cover. A defensible Edmonton plan connects source control, cleaning, concrete repair, coating documents, and seasonal inspection. Distinguish the heated floor from the exposed edge An interior garage bay, overhead-door line, exterior apron, ramp, and wall perimeter may not share the same wetting or freezing exposure. Ask the assessor to divide them on the plan and explain each termination. A system selected for a conditioned interior should not be assumed suitable beyond the door. Coordinate snow removal so blades, chains, and stored piles do not damage terminations or hold salty water against walls. Keep drains and collection points functional through the season. When spring cleaning reveals aggregate loss, hollow patches, widening cracks, or rust staining, pause cosmetic repair and obtain the appropriate concrete evaluation. Updated September 8, 2026 Ask Denis about your floor A workshop floor should be planned around the work, not the showroom photograph. Welding, grinding, oils, cutting fluids, hot parts, jacks, benches, rolling cabinets, compressors, vehicle traffic, and cleaning each create different demands. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/services/commercial-epoxy-flooring
Commercial Epoxy Flooring Edmonton | Final Finish

Warehouses · Showrooms · Industrial Built around your working day. Surface preparation, crack filling, and anti-slip finishes for spaces that have to keep running. The plan starts with how the floor is used, not with a colour. Final Finish · Edmonton What it is Three pieces of work, priced against how the space runs. Commercial work here means surface preparation, crack filling, and anti-slip finishes. Sometimes all three, sometimes one of them. A showroom wants a floor that presents the product. A warehouse wants one that survives wheels and cleaning. The same crew does both, and the difference shows up in the texture and the sequence, not in the sales pitch. When it is the right choice Traffic, cleaning, and the hours you can give up. Three things decide whether a coating is worth it here. Walk the space with the people who use it and the people who clean it. Traffic. Foot routes, carts, pallet jacks, and forklifts all load a floor differently. Cleaning. A coarse anti-slip surface that your machine cannot clean trades one problem for another. Access. Which zones can close, and for how long. That usually sets the whole schedule. If the answer is that nothing can close, say so early. It is a real constraint and it changes the plan. The slip-resistance guide and the warehouse planning guide cover the questions worth raising. Service bays and farm shops have their own guides: auto shops and barns and farm shops . What preparation involves Clearing, then grinding, then the cracks. Nothing can be assessed under a pallet rack. Clearing and protecting stock and equipment is part of the job, and it is often the longest part. Grinding opens the slab. Cosmetic crack filling follows. Joints, old coatings, adhesive, oil, and anything hidden under fixed equipment get recorded as they appear. A condition found after clearing can change the scope, so agree in advance how a change is documented and who signs it off. Where moisture is a question, ask for the method, the locations, and the results rather than a general barrier claim. The moisture-testing guide and concrete solutions both go further into this. What to expect Downtime is a written plan, not a hope. Application is only part of the interruption. Clearing, preparation, repairs, each coat, and reopening are separate stages, and each one has a date. Pedestrian access, rolling loads, cleaning, and putting equipment back do not all resume at once. Your quote should name them separately. Use the downtime planning guide to structure the conversation, and the retail guide if customers walk the space. What we do not promise here No numbers without seeing the floor. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/services/concrete-solutions
Concrete Repair, Levelling and Grinding Edmonton | Final Finish

Repair · Levelling · Diamond grinding The concrete decides what the floor can be. Repair, levelling and restoration, and diamond grinding. This is the work under every finish, and on some floors it is the whole job. Final Finish · Edmonton What it is Three things, and they are not interchangeable. Diamond grinding Opening the surface of the slab with diamond tooling so a coating can bond, and taking off what is already there. The grinding guide covers edges, dust, and what a scope should record. Repair Filling and rebuilding cracks, spalls, and damaged areas. Cosmetic crack filling is part of a coating job. Larger repairs are their own line, with their own material and sequence. Levelling and restoration Bringing a floor back toward flat. Elevation changes, low spots, and a worn-out old surface all make a room harder to use and harder to coat evenly. The levelling guide explains flat versus level. When it is the right choice Sometimes the honest answer is that a coating is not the answer. A coating sits on the concrete. It does not stop movement, it does not stop water, and it does not make unsound concrete sound. A crack that keeps opening is a movement question, not a filler question. Damp that returns after every thaw is a water-entry question, and it needs finding first. Hollow-sounding areas mean the slab has let go underneath, and grinding will not reattach it. A floor that only looks tired is usually the easy case, and grinding plus a coating does exactly what you want. We will tell you which of those we think you have. Where it needs a different trade or a qualified evaluation, we will say that too. What preparation involves Record the floor before anyone chooses a finish. Cracks, spalls, hollow areas, patches, joints, old coatings, oil, adhesive, low spots, and water history. All of it before colour. Some of that is cosmetic and some of it is not, and the two look similar from standing height. Ask how anything discovered after the grind gets photographed, priced, and approved. The concrete condition guide and the repair-mortar guide explain where the line sits. What to expect Dust, noise, and an empty room. Grinding is mechanical work. The space has to be clear, and it stays out of use while the work is on. Where preparation is part of a coating job, the whole installation usually runs two days, and it varies with the concrete. Where repair or levelling is the job, the schedule depends entirely on what the slab needs, and Denis will give you that after he has seen it. What we do not promise here Moisture is a question, not a guarantee. Efflorescence, damp patches, or a floor that was recently flooded are reasons to investigate. They do not identify a source, and no product label settles it. If testing is proposed, ask for the method, the locations, the timing, and the results, plus the product documentation that ties those results to the system going down. A broad moisture-barrier label is not that record. Read the moisture-testing guide before you treat any test as a pass. If you are weighing grinding and polishing against a coating, the polishing comparison keeps that decision on the substrate. If a sealer is the other option, see the sealer comparison . ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/services/garage-floor-coating-edmonton
Garage Floor Coating Edmonton | Final Finish Epoxy

Garage floors · Edmonton A garage floor you can wash off in March. A coated garage floor is a system built on your slab: grinding, crack filling, a flake or metallic field, and a top coat over all of it. Final Finish · Edmonton What it is Not paint. A floor built in layers. Garage floor paint sits on top of the concrete. A coating is bonded into a slab that has been opened by grinding first. That is the whole difference, and it is why preparation takes longer than the colour choice. The build is straightforward. We grind the slab, fill the cracks we can see, lay the coat, broadcast flake into it, scrape it back once it has set, and finish with a top coat. Where a room needs more grip, an anti-slip top coat goes on last. You can see the same sequence on the process page , and the layers in the finish library . The finish comparison sets flake, metallic, and solid colour side by side. When it is the right choice And when something else is. A coating makes sense when The slab is sound, and you want it brighter and easier to wash. Salt, meltwater, and tracked grit are the problem you actually have. You want the garage to work as a shop, a gym, or a room, not only parking. You are tired of a dusty slab that never looks clean. Talk to us about something else when The concrete is moving, heaving, or badly spalled. That is a concrete repair conversation first. Water is coming up through the slab. A coating does not fix a water source. The floor is brand new. Fresh concrete has to cure before anything goes on it; the new concrete guide explains the wait. You want the look for a warehouse or a showroom. The planning is different, so start on the commercial page . Paint, a roll-on kit, and a full coating are three different products at three different levels of work. None of them is right for every garage, and we would rather say so before you book. What preparation involves The grind is the job. Diamond grinding opens the surface of the concrete so the coating has something to hold. It is noisy, dusty work, and it is the part that decides how the floor lasts. Cosmetic crack filling follows the grind. Visible cracks get filled so they do not read through the finish. A crack that turns out to be structural changes the scope, and so does an old coating hiding under the dust. Denis tells you that when he sees it, not after the invoice. Before the estimate, it helps to know what is on the floor now: bare concrete, an old coating, or paint. Oil stains, de-icing residue, and any history of water are all worth mentioning. ## https://www.finalfinishepoxy.ca/services/residential-epoxy-flooring
Residential Epoxy Flooring Edmonton | Final Finish

Barns · Workshops · Basements · Kitchens The rooms in the house nobody finished. Decorative epoxy, flake, and metallic coatings for the concrete rooms you already own. Looking for a garage floor? That has its own page. Final Finish · Edmonton What it is A finish chosen around the room, not a catalogue. Residential work covers barns, workshops, basements, kitchens, and bathrooms. Three finish families are available: decorative epoxy, flake, and metallic. What changes between rooms is not the chemistry. It is the light, the traffic, and what the space has to hold. A barn floor and a basement floor want different things from the same three materials. The guides to kitchen and bathroom floors and barn and farm shop floors go room by room. For a garage, start at the garage floor coating page instead. It covers vehicles, salt, and storage in detail. When each finish is the right choice Pick for the room, then look at colour. Flake A patterned field that hides everyday grit well. Good in a workshop or a barn, where the floor takes real use. See it against your own cabinets and lighting before you commit; the flake and colour guide sets out a sample process. Decorative epoxy A calmer, more even surface. It suits a kitchen, a bathroom, or a basement that reads as a room rather than a shop. Ask how the proposed texture handles wet feet and the cleaning method you actually use. Metallic A poured composition rather than a repeating pattern. Every floor lands differently, so look at samples and agree where the effect stops. The metallic expectations guide covers what to ask. The finish library shows all three families, and the floor visualizer puts them on a photo of your own room. The finish comparison weighs them against each other. What preparation involves The slab decides more than the colour does. Grinding comes first. It opens the concrete so the coating bonds, and it is the same step in every room we work in. Cosmetic crack filling follows. Interior rooms bring their own questions: an old coating under the lino, a patch where a wall used to be, a low spot that pools when you mop. Mention water history early. A coating is not a fix for water coming through a slab, and finding that out after the grind helps nobody. Photos are enough to start the conversation. The site-assessment checklist lists what to record, and concrete solutions goes into repair and levelling. What to expect Two days, give or take the concrete. Installation usually runs two days, and it varies with the slab. An interior room also has to be emptied, and grinding is loud and dusty. Talk through access before the date is set. A basement means carrying equipment down stairs, and a kitchen means the room is out of use while the work is on. Both are easier to plan for than to find out on the day. What we do not promise here Ask for the specifics in writing. No price, no return-to-use time, and no coverage term appears on this page. Those belong to your floor, and they are written into your quote. Two more things this page will not claim. A coating is not slip-proof, and the right texture depends on footwear, water, and how you clean. A coating also does not replace moisture work, ventilation, or heating; it is one part of a room. Epoxy Floor Warranty | Final Finish Edmonton

Written with the quote Warranty is a document, not a slogan. This site will not invent a year count or a lifetime promise. What is covered for preparation, coating, and wear is written into the quote Denis sends you. Final Finish · Edmonton What you can expect The quote names the terms. A manufacturer's product sheet and an installer's workmanship are two different things. Final Finish will say which is which, in writing, before work starts. If a number is not in your quote, it is not a promise, and you should not accept it as one from us or from anybody else. Workmanship coverage is stated on the quote for that job. Product limits follow the system that was actually installed. Abuse, unapproved chemicals, moisture that was never disclosed, and later trades cutting the floor all sit outside a coating warranty.
